movements.heading: Remembering why I was made
lines: Father, you made me for your glory.
If my life is not offered back to you, I am missing the reason I exist.
I do not want to live as though I belong to myself, or as though my gifts, time, and choices are mainly for my own comfort.
Make me a willing instrument in your hands, so that my life points back to you.
themes: Human beings are created for God's glory, not self-ownership or self-exaltation.
A life disconnected from God's purpose is empty, however successful it may appear.

scriptures.connection: God speaks of his people as those created for his glory. This grounds the prayer's confession that human life finds its meaning in belonging to God and displaying his worth.
Paul teaches that even ordinary actions are to be done for God's glory. This supports the prayer's desire that the whole life, not only religious moments, be offered to God.

movements.heading: Asking you to keep me from unbelief
lines: Lord, keep me from the deep sin of unbelief.
If being joined to Christ is my greatest good, then pulling away from him in distrust is a terrible evil.
I know I cannot cling to him perfectly in this life.
My faith is weak, my obedience is unfinished, and my heart wanders.
So hold me fast.
Do not let me drift from Christ, and do not let me treat your command to trust him as a small thing.
themes: Union with Christ is the believer's highest good and the source of spiritual life.
Unbelief is not merely weakness or uncertainty; it is a serious turning away from God's command and promise.
The believer depends on God's preserving grace because obedience and faith are imperfect in this life.

scriptures.connection: Jesus describes abiding in him as the only way to bear fruit, because apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This directly supports the prayer's emphasis on union with Christ as essential life and fruitfulness.
This passage warns believers against an unbelieving heart that falls away and calls them to hold fast to Christ. It gives biblical weight to the prayer's plea to be kept from departing from him.

movements.heading: Receiving correction when your gifts become idols
lines: Father, when you take away outward comforts and blessings, teach me to listen.
So often I enjoy your gifts without thanking you, use what I have without serving you, and become settled, proud, and hard.
Good things can quietly become idols in my hands.
They can do damage precisely because they look harmless.
If a blessing is feeding my sin, take away the fuel.
Love me enough to strip away whatever keeps me from loving you rightly.
themes: All blessings come from God and are meant to be received with gratitude and used in his service.
Even lawful blessings can become idols when they make the heart secure apart from God.
God's fatherly discipline may remove comforts in order to expose sin and restore holiness.

scriptures.connection: Moses warns Israel that prosperity can lead the heart to forget God and imagine that blessings came by human strength. This supports the prayer's concern that good gifts can produce pride, hardness, and practical unbelief.
God's discipline is described as fatherly and aimed at sharing his holiness. This helps frame the removal of blessings not as cruelty, but as loving correction meant to produce righteousness.

movements.heading: Choosing holiness over comfort
lines: Teach me to value even a small increase in holiness more than the loss of many comforts.
If losing something helps me glorify you more, then let me see that as mercy, not punishment only.
Make me able to say honestly that gaining more of Christ, more obedience, and more purity is better than keeping everything that makes me spiritually dull.
themes: Holiness is more valuable than earthly security or comfort.
Loss can become gain when it loosens the grip of sin and makes Christ more precious.
The Christian life requires reordering loves so that God is treasured above his gifts.

scriptures.connection: Paul counts former gains as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This supports the prayer's request to prize spiritual gain above outward loss.

Jesus uses severe imagery to teach that anything leading us into sin must be dealt with decisively. This illuminates the prayer's request that God remove whatever fuels sin, even if the removal is painful.

movements.heading: Wanting to love you more
lines: The more I truly love you, the more I see how little I love you.
The more I hunger for you, the more aware I become of how weak and empty I am.
The more my heart breaks over sin, the more I want it to be softened and broken still.
Do not let me be satisfied with shallow love, weak desire, or casual repentance.
Draw me further in.
themes: Growth in grace often increases awareness of remaining sin and need.
True love for God creates a deeper desire to love him more.
Repentance is not a one-time feeling but an ongoing work of a softened heart before God.

scriptures.connection: Jesus blesses those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, promising that God will satisfy them. This supports the prayer's longing for deeper desire and greater holiness.
David speaks of a broken and contrite heart as the kind of response God receives. This grounds the prayer's request for deeper grief over sin without implying despair.
Paul has not yet arrived, but presses on toward Christ. This fits the prayer's sense that real grace produces not complacency, but a longing for more.

movements.heading: Keeping me awake to my sin and close to Christ
lines: My great danger is how quickly I forget my sin.
I forget the sins of my youth, and even the sins of yesterday fade from my mind by today.
Search me and keep me honest.
Keep me from anything that leads me toward unbelief, coldness, or losing the felt nearness of my union with Christ.
Keep me close to him, trusting him, depending on him, and returning to him quickly when I stray.
themes: The heart is prone to forget sin and needs God's searching and preserving grace.
Believers must be guarded from spiritual drift, unbelief, and coldness toward Christ.
The felt enjoyment of union with Christ can be weakened by sin, even though Christ remains the believer's only hope.

scriptures.connection: The psalmist asks God to search him, expose grievous ways, and lead him in the everlasting way. This supports the prayer's plea for honesty about sin and divine keeping.
David asks to be cleansed from hidden faults and kept back from presumptuous sins. This is closely connected to the prayer's concern about forgotten sins and the need for God to restrain the heart.
John warns against denying sin and points believers to confession and God's faithful forgiveness. This supports the prayer's desire to remain awake to sin and quick to return to God.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Letting you search me honestly
lines: All-seeing God, you know me completely.
You see not only what I do, but why I do it.
You know the hidden self-interest, pride, fear, and unbelief that can cling even to the things I call obedience.
I can look at my obvious sins and feel ashamed, but you also see the mixed motives in my prayers, service, and worship.
If even heaven is not pure before you, I have no room to defend myself.
I would run from what I see in my own heart if I could.
themes: God searches the heart and judges motives, not merely outward behaviour.
Even sincere religious duties can be stained by remaining sin.
True prayer begins with honest self-knowledge before God’s holiness.

scriptures.connection: This passage presents God’s word and sight as exposing the thoughts and intentions of the heart, leaving every person fully known before him. It supports the prayer’s refusal to hide behind outward actions.

Isaiah confesses that even the righteous acts of God’s people are polluted when they stand before him in their sin. This helps ground the prayer’s concern that sin can contaminate even duties meant for God.

Job’s friend speaks of God’s purity in comparison with the heavens and human beings. While the speech in Job must be handled carefully, this particular thought reflects the biblical theme of God’s holiness exceeding all created purity.

movements.heading: Trusting the way you made for me to come back
lines: And yet you do not turn away from me in disgust.
You have made a way for me to come home to you.
You gave your Son, and he died so that I could live.
In Jesus, your mercy does not ignore your justice, and your justice does not cancel your mercy.
At the cross, your truth, righteousness, peace, and love are not competing with each other;
they shine together.
themes: God provides reconciliation for sinners through the death of his Son.
The cross upholds God’s righteousness while showing mercy to the guilty.
Salvation is God’s own gracious plan, not human self-rescue.

scriptures.connection: Paul explains that God justifies sinners through Christ’s blood in a way that demonstrates his righteousness. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that God’s honour is not compromised but displayed in forgiving sinners.
The verse poetically joins steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and peace. The prayer sees these realities coming together most fully in God’s saving work through Christ.
Jesus describes the Father’s gift of the Son as the way sinners receive life rather than condemnation. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that God has made a way back through his Son.

movements.heading: Finding everything I lack in Jesus
lines: In Jesus, captives are set free.
The guilty are forgiven.
The unclean are made new.
When I am weak, he is strength that does not run out.
When I am needy, he is wealth I could never measure.
When I am confused and ignorant, he holds the wisdom and knowledge I need.
When I am empty, he is fullness itself.
I do not come to you with anything impressive in my hands.
I come because Christ has everything I need.
themes: Christ is sufficient for every need of salvation and spiritual life.
In Christ believers receive redemption, forgiveness, renewal, strength, wisdom, and fullness.
Human emptiness is answered by the fullness of Christ, not by self-sufficiency.

scriptures.connection: Paul says redemption and forgiveness are found in Christ through his blood, according to God’s grace. This supports the prayer’s confidence that the enslaved and guilty find freedom and pardon in him.
This verse gathers several saving gifts in Christ: wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. It closely matches the prayer’s movement from personal lack to Christ’s complete provision.
Paul describes Christ as the one in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. This grounds the prayer’s claim that ignorance and need are met in him.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers are filled in him. This supports the prayer’s language of fullness for the empty.

movements.heading: Receiving Christ himself, not just his gifts
lines: So when you call me to come, I want to come with open hands.
Help me receive your grace, not reluctantly but gladly.
Teach me not only to accept your mercy, but to rest in it.
Let me not boast in the cross as an idea while keeping my distance from the crucified Savior.
Let my joy be not only that I am forgiven, but that Jesus himself is the one who gave himself for my atonement.
themes: The gospel calls sinners to come to Christ and receive grace by faith.
Faith rests gladly in God’s mercy rather than merely submitting to it with hesitation.
The believer glories not only in the benefits of the cross, but in Christ crucified.

scriptures.connection: Jesus personally calls the weary and burdened to come to him for rest. This supports the prayer’s response to God’s gracious invitation.
John describes receiving Christ and believing in his name as the mark of those who become children of God. This grounds the prayer’s language of taking and receiving grace.
Paul’s only boast is the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ, not religious achievement or human status. This supports the prayer’s desire to glory in the crucified Savior himself.

movements.heading: Resting in what you have secured for me
lines: Father, the blessings you give in Christ are not fragile.
You have provided for my safety, and you have promised to keep me and make me stronger.
I know I cannot be truly settled without the forgiveness of my sins.
I cannot be at ease while my nature remains unchanged.
I cannot have deep peace without the hope of being with you forever.
All of this is mine in your Son, Jesus.
Blessed be his name.
themes: God preserves his people and strengthens them in grace.
Forgiveness, renewal, and hope of eternal life are necessary for true peace.
All saving blessings are held together in Christ.

scriptures.connection: Paul expresses confidence that God will complete the good work he began in believers. This supports the prayer’s trust that God will keep and strengthen his people, not merely start their salvation.
Peter connects new birth, living hope, an imperishable inheritance, and God’s guarding power. This grounds the prayer’s peace in both present keeping and future hope.
Paul describes grace as both saving and training believers for godly lives while they wait for Christ’s appearing. This supports the prayer’s insistence that pardon and renovation belong together.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Your purpose is to make Jesus loved and honored
lines: Father, I believe your great purpose is to make your Son glorious and deeply loved.
Jesus is risen and ascended, and one day all who belong to him will see his glory clearly and love him without end.
My love for him now is small and mixed with so much weakness, but please make that future my own:
to see him, love him, and praise him forever.
themes: God's saving purpose is centered on the glory of Christ.
Christ is ascended and will be adored forever by his people.
The believer longs for fuller love for Christ than is possible in this present weakness.

scriptures.connection: Jesus prays that those the Father has given him would be with him and see his glory. This directly supports the prayer's hope of finally beholding Christ and loving him perfectly.
Paul describes the Father's exaltation of Jesus and the universal confession of his lordship. It grounds the prayer's claim that God's purpose is the glory and honor of Christ.

movements.heading: You have begun in me what you will finish
lines: Even now, you have given me a real beginning.
I do not see Jesus as clearly as I will one day, but you have opened my eyes enough to know him, receive him, trust him, and belong to him.
Teach me to love him not only in private thoughts, but in what I say, how I live, and what I delight in.
themes: God begins the believer's knowledge and love of Christ in this life and will complete it in glory.
Faith receives Christ personally, not merely as an idea.
Love for Christ should shape the heart, speech, and daily life.

scriptures.connection: Paul contrasts our present partial knowledge with the clear knowledge believers will have in the age to come. This supports the prayer's tension between real present faith and future fullness.
Paul speaks of receiving Christ Jesus the Lord and continuing to walk in him. That fits the prayer's movement from receiving Christ to living a life rooted in him.

movements.heading: Let love for Christ shape my worship and obedience
lines: Help me give attention to the practices and patterns that keep my heart near you:
worship, prayer, obedience, self-control, and the steady listening to your Word.
Keep me from doing these things to impress anyone or to earn your favor.
Let me do them because I love Christ, because I am grateful, and because I want to know and keep his will.
themes: Christian discipline and worship are responses of love and gratitude, not attempts to earn salvation.
Obedience flows from love for Christ.
The believer must intentionally guard and cultivate a Christ-centered heart.

scriptures.connection: Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments. This grounds the prayer's desire to seek and obey Christ's will from love rather than mere duty.
Paul urges believers, in view of God's mercy, to offer themselves to God in worshipful obedience. This supports the prayer's emphasis on gratitude as the motive for disciplined devotion.

movements.heading: Make Christ the center of my life and happiness
lines: You have been teaching me that my life and joy are found in belonging to Christ.
Keep my heart and mind centered on him.
Make union with him more precious to me than comfort, approval, success, or control.
And make me more like him
not closed in on myself, but ready to share good with others because he has been so generous to me.
If Christ is mine and I am his, that is already a taste of heaven here on earth.
themes: The believer's deepest identity and joy are found in union with Christ.
Christ is sufficient as the center of the heart and mind.
Union with Christ produces Christlike generosity and love toward others.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes the believer's life as crucified with Christ and now lived by faith in the Son of God. This supports the prayer's language of finding one's life in oneness with Christ.
Paul's statement that to live is Christ expresses the Christ-centered life the prayer asks for: happiness, purpose, and identity gathered into him.
Paul teaches that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works prepared by God. This connects union with Christ to the practical outflow of doing good to others.

movements.heading: Carry me by your Spirit toward the city to come
lines: But Father, I cannot keep walking this road by my own strength.
I need the power, life, and steady prompting of your Spirit to carry me forward.
Keep moving me toward the Jerusalem that is above, toward the home you have promised, when my faith will become sight and my love will be whole.
themes: The Christian life depends on the ongoing work and power of the Holy Spirit.
Believers are pilgrims moving toward the heavenly city God has promised.
Present sanctification is sustained by God, not by self-reliance.

scriptures.connection: Paul teaches that believers put sin to death by the Spirit and are led by the Spirit as God's children. This grounds the prayer's dependence on the Spirit for perseverance and growth.
Hebrews describes believers as having come to the heavenly Jerusalem through Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant. This illuminates the prayer's image of being carried toward the true Jerusalem.

movements.heading: Let me live like Jesus until I die in peace
lines: While I am still in this world, let me represent Jesus faithfully.
Teach me to do what he would have me do, to live in the way he has shown, and to walk with love, gentleness, and humility.
Make my life the kind of life through which others can recognize him.
And when death comes, let me meet it with peace because I have lived and died belonging to Christ.
themes: Christians are called to imitate Christ in ordinary life.
Love, meekness, and humility make Christ visible through his people.
Peace in death rests on belonging to Christ.

scriptures.connection: John says that whoever abides in Christ ought to walk as Jesus walked. This directly supports the prayer's desire to live in the world as Christ would have lived.
Paul calls believers to imitate God as beloved children and walk in love, following Christ's self-giving pattern. This grounds the prayer's emphasis on love and Christlike conduct.
Paul faces life and death with confidence because Christ will be honored in him and death means being with Christ. This supports the prayer's longing for peace at death through belonging to Jesus.

movements.heading: Coming to Christ and nowhere else
lines: Lord God, you have called me to trust in Jesus, and I do.
Keep pulling my heart away from every false place I run for safety.
I do not want another refuge, another cleansing, another foundation, another source of life, or another place to rest.
Let Jesus be enough for me
not just in what I say I believe, but in what I actually depend on when I am afraid, guilty, tired, or tempted.
themes: God commands and enables faith in Christ
Christ alone is the sinner’s refuge, cleansing, foundation, fullness, and rest
Exclusive trust in Jesus rather than self-made securities

scriptures.connection: Peter declares that salvation is found in no one but Jesus. This supports the prayer’s refusal to seek refuge, cleansing, or rescue anywhere else.
Paul teaches that no foundation can be laid other than Jesus Christ. The prayer’s language of building on no other foundation rests on this same Christ-centered confidence.

movements.heading: Receiving both forgiveness and cleansing
lines: Father, at the cross Jesus gave himself completely.
Do not let me separate what you have joined together.
Make me deeply honest about both the guilt of my sin and the way sin stains and twists me.
I need Jesus not only to pardon me, but to change me.
Give me repentance as well as forgiveness.
Teach me to love what is holy, to want a clean heart, to think with the mind of Christ, and to walk in the path he walked.
themes: Christ’s saving work addresses both guilt and corruption
Repentance and forgiveness are gifts found in Christ
Holiness is inseparable from the gospel
The believer is called to Christlike life and obedience

scriptures.connection: This passage presents Jesus as the exalted Leader and Savior who gives both repentance and forgiveness. That directly grounds the prayer’s request for inward turning as well as pardon.

Paul says Christ gave himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works. The prayer’s concern for forgiveness, cleansing, holiness, and practical obedience reflects this full scope of salvation.
Peter describes Christ’s suffering as leaving believers an example to follow. This supports the prayer’s desire to have Christ’s mind and walk in his steps.

movements.heading: Belonging to your wise and gentle care
lines: Do not leave me to run my own life as if I belonged to myself.
Help me rejoice that I am in your hands.
You are wiser than I am, and you do not make mistakes.
You are kinder than my fears imagine, and you do not harm your children.
You are gentle with weak people, and you do not crush those who come to you in need.
Teach me to rest under your care instead of fighting for control.
themes: The believer belongs to God, not to self
God’s providence is wise, kind, and tender
Surrender grows from trust in God’s character

scriptures.connection: Paul reminds believers that they are not their own because they were bought with a price. This grounds the prayer’s surrender of self-disposal to God’s ownership and care.
Jesus invites the weary to come to him and describes himself as gentle and lowly. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God’s rule is not crushing but tender and restful.

movements.heading: Living so others can see Christ clearly
lines: Please keep my attitude, words, and behavior from making Christ look ugly to the people around me.
Let my life make him seem as good and beautiful as he truly is.
Wherever I have the chance, help me do real good to others.
Do not let me walk past opportunities to serve just because they are inconvenient, unnoticed, or costly.
themes: Christian conduct should adorn the gospel rather than discredit it
Believers are called to active goodness and usefulness
Love for neighbor is a visible witness to Christ

scriptures.connection: Paul urges believers to live in a way that adorns the doctrine of God our Savior. This matches the prayer’s desire not to scandalize others but to make Christ attractive through conduct.
Paul calls Christians to do good as they have opportunity, especially to fellow believers. That supports the prayer’s request not to refuse chances for usefulness and mercy.

movements.heading: Using what I have as a steward, not an owner
lines: Teach me to see my money and possessions rightly.
They are not for showing off, feeding pride, or making comfort my god.
They are gifts to support the life you have given me and responsibilities you have entrusted to me.
Help me govern my desires wisely, live honestly, avoid needless debt, and have enough open-handedness to help those in need.
Make mercy and forgiveness feel not like burdens, but like part of the joy of belonging to Jesus.
Shape me so that the world sees something of his likeness in me.
themes: Possessions are entrusted by God for stewardship, not pride or luxury
Financial integrity and generosity belong to Christian discipleship
Mercy and forgiveness reflect the character of Christ
The goal of Christian life is conformity to Jesus

scriptures.connection: Paul’s command to owe no one anything except love directly supports the prayer’s concern for financial integrity while keeping love at the center.
Paul connects honest labor with the ability to share with anyone in need. This grounds the prayer’s desire to handle resources responsibly and generously.
Believers are commanded to be kind, tenderhearted, and forgiving because God has forgiven them in Christ. This supports the prayer’s longing to be merciful and forgiving as a reflection of Jesus.

movements.heading: Coming to the Father with reverent confidence
lines: Father of my Lord Jesus, help me come to you the right way
not casually, not as if I deserve an audience, and not cringing as though you were unwilling to receive me.
Teach me to come with deep reverence and with the honest confidence you give to your children through Christ.
themes: God is holy and not to be approached lightly; yet believers may draw near with confidence because of Christ and their adoption as God’s children.

scriptures.connection: This passage grounds bold access to God in Jesus our great high priest. It holds together reverence before God with confidence that mercy and help are truly available.
Paul contrasts slavery-like fear with the Spirit-given cry of children to their Father. That supports the prayer’s desire for neither presumption nor servile fear, but filial confidence.

movements.heading: Loving the God I cannot fully understand
lines: You are far beyond what I can figure out.
My mind cannot contain you.
But you are not beyond love.
You know that, beneath all the weakness and confusion in me, I love you above everything else, because you are more worthy, more good, more beautiful, and more complete than anything you have made.
themes: God is incomprehensible yet truly knowable in love; love for God is a fitting response to his supreme goodness and perfection.

scriptures.connection: Paul prays that believers would know the love of Christ even though it surpasses knowledge. This supports the prayer’s distinction between what the mind cannot exhaust and what the heart can truly receive and love.
Jesus identifies supreme love for God as the greatest commandment. The prayer’s claim that God is to be loved above all rests on this biblical priority.

movements.heading: Resting in Jesus, who gave himself to me and for me
lines: My heart softens when I look at the love of Jesus.
He came near enough to call me family.
He shared my flesh and blood.
He bound himself to his people in covenant love.
He died for me.
He rose for me.
He belongs to me, and I belong to him
not because I earned him, but because he gave himself to me as well as for me.
I am never more truly myself than when I am his.
When I stop trying to own my life apart from him and lose myself in him, I find the life I was made for.
themes: The incarnation, atonement, resurrection, covenant union with Christ, and belonging to Christ define the believer’s true identity.

scriptures.connection: Hebrews says the Son was not ashamed to call his people brothers and shared in flesh and blood to save them. This grounds the prayer’s language of Jesus’ nearness, kinship, and identification with us.
Paul describes life by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. That directly supports the prayer’s personal trust in Christ’s self-giving love.
Paul uses marriage to speak of Christ’s covenant love for the church and the mystery of union with him. This illuminates the prayer’s language of being bound to Christ and belonging to him.

movements.heading: Asking Jesus’ love to thaw my cold heart
lines: But my love is often cold.
It can feel frozen over
more like ice than fire.
Let the love of Jesus warm me again.
Let it lift the weight I keep carrying.
Let it become a taste of heaven to me now.
Show me more of what his love is doing in me, so that my love for him becomes alive, steady, and wholehearted.
Let the strong tide of his everlasting love rise over the sharp rocks of my sin and my worries.
Keep me from being wrecked on the things that would otherwise break me, and carry my heart above them.
themes: Christ’s love revives cold affections, relieves burdens, assures the believer, and overwhelms sin and anxiety with enduring mercy.

scriptures.connection: John teaches that our love is a response to God’s prior love. The prayer asks for Christ’s love to kindle the believer’s love, which follows that biblical order.

Paul says Christ’s love controls those who understand his death and resurrection, redirecting them away from self-centered living. This supports the prayer’s plea for Christ’s love to become an active force within the heart.
Paul insists that nothing in creation can separate believers from God’s love in Christ. That anchors the image of an everlasting love strong enough to cover sin, care, and danger.

movements.heading: Being changed into the likeness of Christ
lines: Make my life fruitful as I live in that love.
Let my character become more like Christ day by day.
If even the smallest marks of his work can be seen in me, keep working.
Do not stop with a rough beginning.
Shape me with your patient, skilled hand until the likeness of Jesus is clear in me, and I become a faithful reflection of my Master.
themes: Sanctification is God’s ongoing work by which believers bear fruit and are conformed to the image of Christ.

scriptures.connection: This passage describes believers being transformed into the Lord’s image from one degree of glory to another by the Spirit. It directly supports the prayer’s request for progressive Christlikeness.
Paul presents conformity to the image of Christ as God’s purpose for his people. That gives biblical weight to the prayer’s longing to become a true copy or reflection of the Master.
Jesus teaches that fruitfulness comes from abiding in him, not from self-generated effort. This supports the request to become fruitful by living in Christ’s love.

movements.heading: Calling on Father, Son, and Spirit
lines: Lord Jesus, come near to me.
Holy Spirit, rest on me and fill me with your help.
Holy Father, look on me with mercy for the sake of your beloved Son.
themes: The prayer closes by seeking communion with the triune God: Christ’s nearness, the Spirit’s presence, and the Father’s mercy through the beloved Son.

scriptures.connection: Jesus promises the Spirit as Helper and says he will not leave his disciples as orphans. This supports the prayer’s request for both Christ’s nearness and the Spirit’s abiding presence.
Paul speaks of adoption, grace in the Beloved, and redemption through Christ’s blood. This grounds the prayer’s appeal to the Father’s mercy for the sake of his beloved Son.

movements.heading: Asking you to keep my love alive
lines: Lord Jesus, if I truly love you, I will want to look for you and be near you.
But I know I cannot even keep that desire alive on my own.
Keep my love for you from cooling off.
Teach me to seek you because you are good, and because every real good I need is found in you.
themes: Love for Christ is itself sustained by Christ’s grace.
The soul seeks Christ because he is good and is the source of true good.

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitful life with him depends on abiding in him, not on self-generated strength. This grounds the prayer’s confession that even seeking and loving Christ must be sustained by him.
John roots human love for God in God’s prior love. The prayer’s desire to love Jesus does not treat love as self-produced but as a response awakened by grace.

movements.heading: Coming to you though I do not deserve to be welcomed
lines: You would be right not to pay attention to me.
I am sinful, self-centered, and far smaller than I pretend to be.
Yet I still come looking for you.
And when you let me find you, I do not meet consuming anger.
I meet mercy.
You stand between me and the judgment I deserve, like a great rock giving shade in unbearable heat.
Because I belong to you, I can live sheltered in your love.
themes: Human unworthiness and selfishness are real and must be confessed honestly.
Christ shelters his people from wrath and receives them in mercy.
The believer’s safety rests in Christ, not in personal worthiness.

scriptures.connection: Paul connects Christ’s death for sinners with being saved from God’s wrath through him. This directly supports the prayer’s image of Christ standing between the believer and deserved judgment.
Isaiah uses the image of a sheltering refuge and shade in a weary land. The prayer draws on that biblical pattern to speak of Christ as protection and relief for the soul.

movements.heading: Admitting what I become without you
lines: When my mind runs ahead without you, it weaves lies and convinces me they are true.
When my desires move without you, even the things that look religious can be lifeless.
I need you to live in me and keep me close to you.
I do not have the kind of sight that can grasp you by nature.
I live by faith in you
the One I cannot yet see, but whose glory is brighter to me than anything in this world.
themes: Apart from Christ, human reasoning and desires are corrupted by sin.
Religious activity without Christ can be spiritually dead.
The Christian life is lived by faith in the unseen but glorious Christ.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes the Christian life as walking by faith rather than by sight. This supports the prayer’s confession that the believer depends on faith in Christ rather than natural spiritual perception.
Peter speaks to believers who love and trust Christ though they do not see him now. That fits the prayer’s focus on loving the unseen Christ whose glory outshines all else.

Hebrews describes Christ’s blood cleansing the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. This helps explain the prayer’s concern that activity apart from Christ, even if outwardly religious, is spiritually empty.

movements.heading: Giving you all the glory
lines: When I see how much sin is still in me, let me admit that the shame is mine.
And when I see anything good, let me know where it comes from:
all goodness is in you, and all glory belongs to you.
Do not let me dress up my pride as spirituality.
Strip away every excuse I use to claim credit for what only your grace can do.
themes: Sin and shame belong to the sinner, while all true good comes from Christ.
God receives the glory for salvation and holiness.
Humility means refusing to take credit for grace.

scriptures.connection: Paul’s confession that nothing good dwells in his flesh reflects the prayer’s honest view of remaining sin. It supports the distinction between what belongs to the sinner by nature and what must come from God.

Paul teaches that Christ himself is the believer’s righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so boasting belongs only in the Lord. This grounds the prayer’s insistence that all good and glory are Christ’s.

movements.heading: Learning to recognize true grace
lines: Keep me from thinking you are most present just because I feel something unusual or impressive inside me.
Do not let me mistake a strange brightness in my heart for the real work of grace.
Show me that your clearest work is often this:
you make my own glory grow dim, and you make the honor, pleasure, and success of this world lose their power over me.
Let your glory rise before me until everything else looks small.
Make me poor in spirit.
Help me find my treasure, my safety, and my good in you.
themes: Spiritual experiences must be tested by whether they exalt Christ rather than the self.
True grace humbles the believer and weakens the world’s grip.
Christ’s glory outshines creation and becomes the believer’s true good.

scriptures.connection: Paul counts former gains as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This supports the prayer’s request that worldly honor and pleasure be eclipsed by Christ’s glory.
Jesus blesses the poor in spirit, those who come empty-handed before God. This illuminates the prayer’s desire to be humbled rather than impressed with personal spiritual experience.
Paul boasts only in the cross, through which the world is crucified to him and he to the world. This fits the prayer’s longing for Christ to eclipse personal glory and worldly goods.

movements.heading: Resting everything in you
lines: So teach me to distrust myself in the right way
not with despair, but with clear eyes.
Let me stop treating myself as my refuge, wisdom, or righteousness.
Let me see that everything I need is in you, and let me gladly live from your fullness.
Amen.
themes: Self-distrust is not despair but humility before Christ.
Christ is the believer’s sufficient wisdom, righteousness, refuge, and life.

scriptures.connection: This passage calls God’s people to trust the Lord rather than lean on their own understanding. It supports the prayer’s request for a humble distrust of self and a settled reliance on God.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers have been filled in him. This directly grounds the final request to find one’s all in Christ.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Remembering what Jesus has already done and what he promised
lines: Lord Jesus, Son of God and Son of Man, you came into our flesh for me.
You suffered, died, rose from the dead, and went back to the Father for my salvation.
Your leaving was not you abandoning me;
it was your promise that you will come back.
Through your Word, your promises, and the meal you gave your church, you keep putting your death before me until the day I see you.
themes: The incarnation, suffering, resurrection, and ascension of Christ are not isolated events but the saving work of the Lord who will return.
Christ’s ascension is a pledge of his return, not a sign that he has left his people behind.
The Lord’s Supper proclaims Christ’s death while the church waits for his coming.

scriptures.connection: Jesus speaks of going to prepare a place for his people and returning to take them to himself, which grounds the prayer’s confidence that his departure is not abandonment.
At the ascension, the angels tell the disciples that Jesus will return in the same way he was taken up, connecting his going away directly with the promise of his coming again.
Paul teaches that the Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes, which supports the prayer’s link between Christ’s death, the sacraments, and watchful hope.

movements.heading: Not being afraid of the day you return
lines: That day does not have to terrify me, because you have bought me back by your death.
Your Spirit lives in me.
Your love keeps my heart alive.
Your Word teaches me how to walk.
I have put my trust in you, and you have not failed me.
I have waited for you, and my waiting has not been wasted.
themes: Christ’s return is not horror for those who belong to him, because redemption, the Spirit’s presence, divine love, and Scripture give assurance.
Faith in Christ is not misplaced trust; he preserves those who entrust themselves to him.
Christian waiting is active hope, not empty delay.

scriptures.connection: Paul ties the believer’s hope in Christ’s appearing to the fact that Jesus gave himself to redeem and purify his people, which explains why his return can be welcomed rather than dreaded.
The Spirit assures believers of their adoption and inheritance with Christ, giving a firm basis for confidence as they look toward the future.
Paul expresses confidence that Christ is able to guard what has been entrusted to him, matching the prayer’s confession that trusting Christ is never finally disappointed.

movements.heading: Hoping for the resurrection of my body
lines: When you come, you will raise this body from the dust and join body and soul together again.
You will do it by your endless power and love.
You already hold the seas in place, move the tides, keep the stars where they belong, and give life to every living thing;
raising me will not be beyond you.
What is perishable in me will be made whole forever.
What is mortal will be clothed with life.
What is weak, dishonored, and worn down will be raised strong, glorious, and fit for your kingdom.
themes: The Christian hope is bodily resurrection, not escape from creation or the permanent separation of body and soul.
God’s sovereign power over creation assures the believer that resurrection is not impossible for him.
The resurrection body will be transformed from mortality, weakness, and dishonor into immortality, power, and glory.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes the resurrection body in contrasts of perishability and imperishability, dishonor and glory, weakness and power, directly grounding this section’s hope.
This passage teaches that the mortal must put on immortality, giving biblical shape to the prayer’s confidence in bodily transformation at Christ’s coming.
Paul says that the returning Savior will transform our lowly bodies to be like his glorious body by his power, connecting resurrection hope to Christ’s return and sovereign ability.

movements.heading: Trusting that your people will share your life and victory
lines: I can rejoice in your promises now, even before I see them fulfilled.
You are the living Head of your people, and you will not leave your body dead in the grave.
Past death there will be resurrection.
Past resurrection there will be judgment.
And for those who are yours, there will be acquittal, peace, and a share in your reign.
themes: Believers can rejoice now in promises that will be fully seen later.
Union with Christ means his life secures the future life of his people.
The last things include resurrection, judgment, vindication in Christ, and participation in his kingdom.

scriptures.connection: Christ is called the head of the body, the church, and the firstborn from the dead; this supports the prayer’s logic that the living Head guarantees life for his members.
Paul argues that no charge can finally stand against God’s elect because Christ died, was raised, and intercedes, grounding the prayer’s hope of acquittal after judgment.
This passage connects dying and living with Christ with future reigning with him, supporting the prayer’s expectation of dominion shared with Christ.

movements.heading: Asking to be kept watchful and faithful
lines: Lord, nothing in my life will be hidden from you.
You will deal truly with all of it:
the sins of my younger years, the sins no one else saw, the times I misused your kindness, ignored your Word, pushed away faithful correction, and went against my conscience.
Let that sober me without driving me away from you.
After your judgment, bring me into the peace and rest, the life and service, the work and joy you have prepared for your chosen people.
Keep me in this faith.
Keep my eyes lifted for Christ’s return.
themes: Final judgment will bring every sin and hidden thing into the light before God.
The believer’s honesty about sin rests alongside confidence in Christ’s mercy and final vindication.
The hope of Christ’s return calls for perseverance, watchfulness, and faithful service until he comes.

scriptures.connection: Paul teaches that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, which grounds the prayer’s sober awareness that every part of life will be dealt with by God.
This passage emphasizes that God will bring every deed, including hidden things, into judgment, fitting the prayer’s naming of secret and conscience-violating sins.
John’s vision includes God’s servants worshiping and reigning in the renewed creation, supporting the prayer’s hope of rest, service, enjoyment, and life after judgment.
John urges believers to abide in Christ so they may have confidence at his appearing, which supports the final request to be kept in faith while looking for Christ’s return.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Asking to be filled with you
lines: Holy Spirit, just as the sun is full of light, the sea is full of water, and heaven is full of glory, make my heart full of you.
Do not let me live on the edges of your presence.
Fill the empty places in me with your life, your holiness, your comfort, and your power.
themes: The Holy Spirit personally indwells and fills believers.
The Christian life depends on the Spirit’s active presence, not merely on religious effort.
God’s fullness is abundant and life-giving.

scriptures.connection: Paul commands believers to be filled with the Spirit, showing that the Christian life is meant to be lived under the Spirit’s ongoing influence and control.
This passage teaches that belonging to Christ includes the indwelling of the Spirit, whose presence gives life even to mortal people.

movements.heading: Needing you to make Christ real to me
lines: All the love the Father has planned, and all that Jesus has done to redeem me, must be made alive in me by your work.
Open my eyes to see Jesus clearly.
Make the unseen things of God more real to me than the loud and temporary things in front of me.
Give me new life where I am dead, sight where I am blind, and faith where I cannot see.
themes: The Spirit applies the saving work of Christ to believers.
Regeneration is the Spirit’s work.
The Spirit reveals Christ and enables spiritual understanding.

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that entrance into God’s kingdom requires birth by the Spirit, grounding the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit for new life.
Jesus says the Spirit will guide his people into truth and glorify Christ, which directly supports the request to see Jesus clearly through the Spirit’s work.
Paul contrasts visible, temporary things with unseen, eternal realities, matching the prayer’s longing to perceive and live by the realities God reveals.

movements.heading: Confessing how empty and sluggish I am
lines: I confess that I am often cold toward you.
I feel poor in spirit, empty, half-awake, and slow to serve.
My prayers can be words without heart.
My praise can be sound without wonder.
I can look at glory and barely see it.
Please do not let me grieve you, ignore you, or push back against your work in me.
themes: Honest confession of spiritual coldness and weakness.
Believers can grieve or resist the Spirit’s work.
True worship and prayer require the Spirit’s life in the heart.

scriptures.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, which supports the prayer’s concern about resisting or dulling the Spirit’s work.
Paul says the Spirit helps believers in their weakness, especially in prayer, which speaks to the confession of weak and inadequate praying.

movements.heading: Come and do your full work in me
lines: Come with power, and drive out every sinful desire that still tries to rule me.
Take the throne in my heart and keep me belonging to Christ.
Come as my teacher, and lead me into truth.
Help me understand what I cannot grasp on my own.
Come as the love of God poured into me, so that I may adore the Father and love him as my greatest treasure.
Come as joy, living in me, stirring me, strengthening me, and making obedience more than duty.
Come as light, opening Scripture to me and shaping my life by what you show me there.
Come as the one who makes me holy.
Let my body, soul, mind, desires, habits, and choices be yours.
Come as my helper.
Strengthen me, guard me, and guide my steps today.
Come as the one who brings beauty out of disorder.
Put what is confused in me back into your order.
Make what is chaotic in me become Christlike and whole.
themes: The Spirit empowers believers to put sin to death.
The Spirit teaches, guides, and illumines Scripture.
The Spirit pours God’s love into the heart and produces joy.
Sanctification involves the whole person being set apart for God.
The Spirit helps, strengthens, and directs believers in daily obedience.

scriptures.connection: Paul says believers put sinful deeds to death by the Spirit and are led by the Spirit, grounding the prayer’s request for power over sin and daily direction.
Jesus identifies the Holy Spirit as the Helper who teaches and reminds his people of Christ’s words, supporting the prayer’s request for instruction and help.
Paul says God’s love is poured into believers’ hearts through the Holy Spirit, which directly supports the request to love and adore the Father by the Spirit’s work.
The psalmist asks God to open his eyes to behold his Word, fitting the prayer’s request for the Spirit to illuminate Scripture and shape obedience.
Paul prays for complete sanctification and grounds it in God’s faithfulness, supporting the prayer’s desire for the whole person to belong to God.

movements.heading: Make your glory visible in me
lines: Holy Spirit, show me more of your glory by making more of your life visible in me.
Let your work in me honor you.
Make my life carry the fragrance of Christ, so that what comes from me is not the stale smell of self, but the clean, living evidence that you are present.
themes: The Spirit glorifies God by transforming believers.
Christian character is meant to display Christ.
The believer’s life can become a witness to the presence and work of God.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes believers being transformed into the image of the Lord by the Spirit, which supports the prayer’s request that the Spirit be magnified through inward change.
Paul uses the image of the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ spreading through God’s people, fitting the prayer’s desire to carry the aroma of Christ in daily life.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)

movements.heading: Asking for the Spirit himself
lines: Lord God, I don’t want to settle for asking only for better habits, stronger feelings, or isolated gifts from you.
I need the Holy Spirit himself.
I feel how easily I run on my own energy, my own instincts, and my own ideas, even when I am doing religious things.
Please give me the real power of his presence, not just faint wishes for change.
If I have him, I have the life and grace he brings.
themes: The believer’s need is not merely for spiritual benefits but for the personal presence and work of the Holy Spirit.
True Christian life cannot be produced by natural ability or religious effort alone.

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches believers to ask the Father for the Holy Spirit, grounding this request in God’s willingness to give what his children most deeply need.

Paul presents the Spirit’s indwelling as essential to belonging to Christ and sharing in resurrection life, which fits the prayer’s longing for the Spirit himself rather than mere outward improvements.

movements.heading: Not settling for a small measure
lines: Save me from being satisfied with only a little awareness of your Spirit’s work.
Save me from the unbelief that assumes you will not give more of yourself.
When my heart is dull, don’t let me make peace with that dullness.
When I mistake a little insight, a little discipline, or a little comfort for fullness of life in you, wake me up and draw me further in.
themes: Spiritual complacency is a real danger, especially when small evidences of grace become an excuse not to seek God more earnestly.
Faith expects God to be generous, not reluctant, in giving his Spirit and deepening his work.

scriptures.connection: Paul prays for believers who already belong to Christ to be strengthened by the Spirit and to know more deeply the love of Christ, showing that Christians may rightly seek a fuller experience of God’s work in them.
Paul confronts the mistake of beginning by the Spirit but trying to continue by human effort, which speaks directly to the prayer’s confession of self-reliance.

movements.heading: Trusting what the Spirit can do
lines: Holy Spirit, you can do what I cannot do for myself.
You can heal what is broken in me, help me where I am weak, bring life where I am spiritually sluggish, and humble me without destroying me.
You can make grace real and active in me.
Because you are the eternal Spirit of God, your work is not shallow or temporary.
Please work in me deeply, effectively, and for the long haul.
themes: The Holy Spirit gives life, renews the heart, and produces real holiness.
Sanctification is God’s effective work in the believer, not self-improvement detached from grace.

scriptures.connection: Jesus identifies the Spirit as the one who gives life, which supports the prayer’s confidence that spiritual renewal depends on the Spirit’s power.
Paul describes believers being transformed by the Lord who is the Spirit, connecting the Spirit’s presence with real change into Christlikeness.

movements.heading: Learning how to seek you when I feel empty
lines: When I feel the lack of your Spirit, give me light and faith instead of panic or passivity.
When I cannot see you clearly, I am easily confused.
Sometimes darkness makes me despair;
other times Satan, my own gifts, or a small amount of spiritual light convince me that I have enough.
Teach me what to do.
Should I simply bow low before you?
Should I stir up my heart and use every good means you have given
prayer, Scripture, worship, repentance, fellowship
without trusting those things in themselves?
Teach me to use them while depending on you alone for the blessing.
themes: Spiritual dryness should lead to humble dependence rather than despair or complacency.
God commonly works through appointed means, but the believer must not trust the means apart from God himself.
Discernment is needed when subjective feelings of God’s absence are mixed with temptation, weakness, and self-reliance.

scriptures.connection: The psalmist cries out from spiritual distress and asks God for guidance, deliverance, and the teaching of his Spirit, closely matching the prayer’s plea for light when God feels hidden.
James holds together resisting the devil, drawing near to God, and humbling oneself, which speaks to the prayer’s concern about Satan’s influence and the need to seek God actively.
Scripture is presented as God-given and sufficient to equip his people, supporting the prayer’s desire to use God’s appointed means while depending on him for their fruit.

movements.heading: Finding the fullness of the Spirit in Jesus
lines: Father, teach me whether I am wrong to ask for the fullness of the Spirit, and correct me if I am looking for it in the wrong place.
I do not want to measure the Spirit’s presence only by what I can feel inside myself.
If I feel empty, let that emptiness drive me to Christ, not into self-obsession.
Teach me that the Spirit does not lead me away from Jesus but makes Jesus everything to me
my life, my joy, my righteousness, my strength, and my home.
Let me know the fullness of the Spirit by trusting and resting in Christ, in whom all fullness is found.
themes: The fullness of the Spirit is not an independent spiritual experience detached from Christ.
The Spirit glorifies Christ and unites believers to him as the source of life, joy, and sufficiency.
Subjective experience matters, but it must be interpreted by faith in Christ rather than by inward sensation alone.

scriptures.connection: Jesus says the Spirit will glorify him and take what is his and declare it to his people, showing that the Spirit’s fullness is Christ-centered rather than self-focused.
Paul teaches that the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers are filled in him, directly supporting the prayer’s final request to find fullness only in Jesus.
Jesus describes abiding in him as the necessary condition for fruitfulness, which fits the prayer’s desire to locate life and strength outside the self and in Christ.

movements.heading: Asking Jesus to fill me with his Spirit
lines: Lord Jesus Christ, fill me with your Spirit.
Make me aware of his presence, not as an idea I mention, but as the living help I need right now.
I am blind without him, so open my eyes.
I am dark inside without your light, so let him speak light into me.
themes: Dependence on Christ to give the Spirit
Spiritual blindness apart from God’s illumination
The Spirit’s personal presence and work in the believer

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that the Spirit guides believers into truth and glorifies Christ by taking what is Christ’s and making it known. This grounds the prayer for the Spirit to make Christ real and present to the believer.

Paul connects God’s original command for light to the inner illumination that reveals the glory of God in Christ. That directly supports the prayer’s cry for God to bring light into spiritual darkness.

movements.heading: Help me see what is already mine in you
lines: Give me faith to see what I so easily forget:
that I am held by you, known by you, and not lost to you;
that my whole self, body and soul, has been bought by your blood;
and that my guilt is covered, not by anything I have done, but by your perfectly obedient life given for me.
themes: Faith receiving Christ’s finished work
Redemption through Christ’s blood
Christ’s righteousness covering the sinner
Assurance of belonging to Christ

scriptures.connection: This passage states that redemption and forgiveness come through Christ’s blood according to God’s grace, supporting the prayer’s confidence that the believer belongs to Christ because he has paid the cost.

Paul contrasts Adam’s disobedience with Christ’s obedience, showing that Christ’s righteous obedience is counted for his people. This grounds the prayer’s trust that sin is covered by Christ’s life, not personal merit.

God speaks of his people as engraved on his hands, an image of permanent covenant remembrance. The prayer uses that kind of assurance to ask for faith to know that Christ will not forget or abandon his own.

movements.heading: Let me know how deeply I am joined to you
lines: Keep filling me with the Spirit’s revealing grace, so I truly understand that nothing can tear me away from you.
Let me know that you have bound me to yourself forever
with righteousness, love, mercy, and faithfulness.
Teach me to live as someone joined to you:
like a branch living from the vine, like a house standing because its foundation is solid.
themes: Indissoluble union with Christ
Covenant love and faithfulness
Christ as the source and foundation of the believer’s life

scriptures.connection: Jesus describes believers as branches that can bear fruit only by abiding in him, which fits the prayer’s image of life flowing from union with Christ.
God promises to betroth his people to himself in righteousness, steadfast love, mercy, and faithfulness. The prayer draws on this covenant language to express permanent belonging to Christ.
Paul says that Jesus Christ is the only foundation that can be laid. This supports the prayer’s image of the believer resting on Christ as a building rests on its foundation.

movements.heading: Make your Spirit my comfort, strength, and life
lines: Let your Spirit comfort me when I am sorrowful, strengthen me when I am under pressure, and renew me when I am tired.
Make his presence in me bear real fruit:
holiness that is not pretend, peace that holds, joy that lasts, prayer that keeps returning to you, and love for you that does not burn out.
themes: The Spirit’s comfort in sorrow
Strength for trials
Fruitfulness in holiness
Peace, joy, prayer, and devotion produced by the Spirit

scriptures.connection: Paul prays that believers would abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit, linking the Spirit’s work with joy, peace, and sustaining confidence in God.
The fruit of the Spirit describes the kind of character and life the prayer asks God to produce—real holiness expressed in love, joy, peace, and other Spirit-formed virtues.
Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray. This supports the request for the Spirit to keep prayer alive even in weariness and need.

movements.heading: Search me so I run to Christ, not myself
lines: Send your Spirit to search my heart.
Show me more honestly where sin still twists me and how helpless I am apart from you.
Do not let that knowledge drive me into despair or self-repair.
Let it drive me to you
to run to you, hold on to you, and rest on you as the beginning, middle, and end of my salvation.
themes: The Spirit’s convicting work
Honest self-knowledge before God
Repentance that flees to Christ
Christ as the whole source of salvation

scriptures.connection: Jesus says the Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. This grounds the prayer for the Spirit to expose sin truthfully rather than leave the heart self-deceived.
The psalmist asks God to search him and reveal any grievous way in him so that God may lead him rightly. This parallels the prayer’s request for heart-searching that results in returning to God.
Jesus is described as the founder and perfecter of faith, which supports the prayer’s confession that salvation depends on Christ from start to finish.

movements.heading: Keep me from resisting the Spirit
lines: Please do not let me treat your Spirit with indifference, push him away through stubbornness, or give him a cold welcome while pretending to want you.
Soften what is hard in me.
Wake up what is sluggish.
Bring me under your gracious rule.
Lord, answer me for the honor of your great name.
themes: Warning against grieving or resisting the Holy Spirit
Need for a softened and responsive heart
God’s glory as the ground of prayer

scriptures.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, especially in the context of sinful patterns that contradict their new life. This supports the prayer’s concern not to respond to the Spirit with coldness or rebellion.

Stephen describes hard-hearted resistance to the Holy Spirit, showing that rebellion against God’s voice is a serious spiritual danger. The prayer turns that warning into a plea for mercy and softness.
God promises to replace a heart of stone with a heart of flesh and put his Spirit within his people. This supports the request for God to soften the heart and make obedience possible by the Spirit.
