movements.heading: Praising your love shown in Jesus
lines: Gracious God, my heart praises you for the astonishing love you have shown me in Jesus.
He is your beloved Son, and yet for me he became human, was rejected, carried sin, and died on the cross.
In him, your grace toward rebels like me has gone beyond anything I could have imagined.
Father, teach me to love you in response to that kind of love.
themes: God’s love is most clearly revealed in the giving of his Son for sinners.
Jesus is both the beloved Son of the Father and the crucified sin-bearer for the guilty.
The right response to redeeming love is worship and love back to God.

scriptures.connection: Paul grounds God’s love not in human worthiness but in Christ’s death for the ungodly. This supports the prayer’s wonder that God loved rebels through the crucified Christ.
Isaiah describes the Servant as rejected and bearing the sins of others. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s confession that Jesus was despised, crucified, and carrying sin for his people.

movements.heading: Asking you to open my hard heart
lines: My heart can be cold and stubborn.
Let your love soften what is hard in me and open what I keep locked shut.
Father, I worship you for giving Jesus.
Lord Jesus, I thank you for laying down your life for me.
Holy Spirit, I thank you for making this good news real to me and not leaving it as words I could hear but never understand.
Let Jesus see the fruit of his suffering in my life.
themes: The human heart needs God’s gracious work to be softened and opened.
The Father gives the Son, the Son gives himself, and the Spirit reveals Christ to the believer.
Christ’s saving suffering bears fruit in those he redeems.

scriptures.connection: God promises to replace a heart of stone with a living heart and to put his Spirit within his people. This directly supports the prayer’s plea for God to soften and open a resistant heart.

Paul teaches that the Spirit enables believers to understand what God has freely given them. This fits the prayer’s thanksgiving that the Spirit reveals the mystery of Christ rather than leaving the sinner blind to it.

The suffering Servant is promised that he will see the outcome of his suffering and be satisfied. The prayer echoes this by asking that Christ’s work would bear visible fruit in the life of the one praying.

movements.heading: Turning from false confidence to Christ alone
lines: Pull me away from every false thing I lean on, and bring me to rest in Christ alone.
Do not let me treat his worth as something ordinary.
Do not let me be unmoved by his blood.
Make me want the cleansing only he can give, and make me honest about how deeply I need it.
themes: Salvation rests in Christ alone, not in human merit or self-made security.
Christ’s blood cleanses the conscience and removes guilt.
True faith includes a serious desire to be cleansed, not merely excused.

scriptures.connection: Paul rejects every ground of confidence apart from being found in Christ with the righteousness that comes through faith. This supports the prayer’s movement away from false trusts and toward Christ alone.

Hebrews presents Christ’s blood as able to purify the conscience for service to the living God. This grounds the prayer’s desire not to be indifferent to Christ’s blood but to seek real cleansing through him.

movements.heading: Giving myself wholly to my Redeemer
lines: Lord Jesus, my Master, Redeemer, and Savior, come and take full possession of me.
You bought me;
I belong to you.
Hold me in your love and overcome my stubborn will.
Take every part of me
my mind, my desires, my words, my hands, my plans
and make them holy and useful to you.
themes: Believers belong to Christ because he purchased them by his death.
Christ’s loving lordship subdues the will without ceasing to be love.
Sanctification includes the whole person being set apart for God’s use.

scriptures.connection: Paul tells believers that they are not their own because they were bought with a price, and therefore must glorify God with their bodies. This directly supports the prayer’s surrender of the whole self to Christ by right of purchase.
Paul urges believers, in view of God’s mercies, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. This illuminates the prayer’s desire for every faculty and action to be consecrated to God.

movements.heading: Remembering how you have not failed me
lines: I am not ashamed of the hope I have placed in you.
Trusting you has not left me disgraced.
I brought you my countless sins, and you put them away.
I trusted you when trouble surrounded me, and you brought me into a spacious place.
I trusted you in distress, even when my faith was shaking, and you did not fail me.
themes: Hope in God is not finally put to shame.
God forgives sins and removes guilt from his people.
God’s faithfulness holds the believer even when faith is weak and trembling.

scriptures.connection: Paul connects justification, hope, suffering, endurance, and God’s love poured into believers’ hearts through the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s confidence that hope in God does not end in shame, even through distress.
Hezekiah speaks of God putting his sins behind his back after deliverance. This is an apt background for the prayer’s gratitude that God has dealt decisively with innumerable sins.
David remembers God drawing him out of overwhelming danger and bringing him into a broad place. This supports the prayer’s testimony that God delivered him when troubles closed in.

movements.heading: Adoring the God who chose, bought, and called me
lines: God of eternal mercy, God who chose me before I ever chose you, God who bought back what sin had ruined through the cross of Christ, God who called me with power I could not create in myself
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I worship you.
Glory, honor, majesty, power, and dominion belong to you forever.
Amen.
themes: Salvation begins in God’s electing grace, is accomplished through Christ’s cross, and is applied by God’s effective call.
The triune God receives worship for the whole work of redemption.
Christian assurance rests in God’s initiative and power, not in human self-rescue.

scriptures.connection: This passage traces salvation from the Father’s choosing, through redemption in Christ’s blood, to the sealing work of the Holy Spirit. It strongly supports the prayer’s final Trinitarian praise for election, purchase, and calling.
Paul links God’s foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification as one saving work of God. This grounds the prayer’s adoration of God’s eternal choice and effectual call.
Jude ends with worship to the God who is able to keep his people and bring them safely into glory. This fits the prayer’s closing doxology of majesty, power, and dominion.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Remembering who you are and admitting what I am
lines: Father, you made everything and you hold everything together.
The rhythm of day and night belongs to you.
The sky above me and the ground under my feet keep speaking of your greatness.
And still, I have sinned against you.
I have pushed back against what my conscience knew was right.
I have treated your commands as if they were optional.
I have heard the good news of Christ and still resisted its call on my life.
Yet you have not left me without hope.
You have given me a real hope in your mercy, and I come to you because of it.
themes: God is Creator and Sustainer of all things; creation displays his glory.
Sin is not merely weakness but resistance to conscience, God's law, and the gospel.
The believer approaches God through hope given by grace, not through personal worthiness.

scriptures.connection: This passage presents creation as a continual witness to God's glory, which grounds the prayer's opening awareness that heaven and earth belong to God and declare his greatness.
Paul teaches that conscience bears witness to moral reality, which supports the confession that sin can involve resisting what one knows inwardly to be right.
Peter describes believers as born again to a living hope through Christ's resurrection, matching the prayer's confidence that even confessed sin is met under God's given hope.

movements.heading: Asking to want holiness more than the world
lines: Please pull my heart away from the attitudes and desires that belong to this passing world.
You have given me new birth from above, and my future is with you in glory.
So teach me to see holiness not as a burden, but as the true beauty of a soul made alive by you.
Make me want what is clean, true, and pleasing to you.
Let holiness become something I love, not merely something I know I should choose.
themes: New birth changes a person's identity and direction.
Because the believer belongs to the coming glory, worldly desires must be resisted.
Holiness is not merely duty but the fitting beauty of a life restored to God.

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that entrance into God's kingdom requires being born from above by the Spirit, which supports the prayer's appeal to a new identity and new desires.
Paul connects union with the risen Christ and future glory with seeking the things above rather than living by earthly desires.
Peter calls believers, as obedient children, not to be shaped by former passions but to be holy because God is holy, directly grounding this request for holiness.

movements.heading: Staying awake in a dangerous world
lines: Do not let me drift into spiritual sleep.
Keep me from becoming careless, dull, or comfortable with sin.
Guard the assurance you have given me, and when it grows weak, draw me back to what is true in Christ.
I am walking through enemy territory, so help me not to move through life unarmed.
Keep me alert to temptation, lies, pride, fear, and whatever would pull me away from you.
Teach me to depend on the protection you provide, not on my own strength.
themes: The Christian life requires vigilance because temptation and spiritual opposition are real.
Assurance is a gift to be guarded by returning to God's promises in Christ.
God provides spiritual armor for believers who cannot stand in their own strength.

scriptures.connection: Paul commands believers to be strong in the Lord and to put on God's armor because spiritual opposition is real, which directly supports the prayer's request to remain armed in enemy territory.
Peter warns Christians to be sober-minded and watchful against the devil's hostility, grounding the prayer's plea not to become spiritually sleepy or careless.
Paul describes the Spirit bearing witness that believers are God's children, which supports the prayer's concern that assurance be preserved and renewed by God.

movements.heading: Trusting you in every circumstance
lines: Make me ready for whatever you place in front of me.
When life is ordinary, keep me faithful.
When life is painful, keep my mind steady on you.
When trials come, do not let them be wasted in me.
Use hardship to humble me, deepen me, and teach me gratitude.
Help me see, even if only later, how you are working through what I would never have chosen.
Let my difficulties lead me to praise you for your wisdom and care.
themes: God is able to fit his people for every circumstance they face.
Trials can become instruments of growth under God's providence.
A mind fixed on God can remain steady even in trouble.

scriptures.connection: Isaiah speaks of God keeping in peace the one whose mind is stayed on him, which supports the request for a steady mind in changing circumstances.
Paul teaches that God works all things for the good of those who love him, with the goal of conforming them to Christ, grounding the prayer's hope that trials can become blessings by God's design.
James explains that testing produces steadfastness and maturity, which supports the prayer's desire that hardship not be wasted but used to form the believer.

movements.heading: Letting your truth reshape my obedience
lines: Straighten out the way I think.
Let your truth become clear to me, consistent in me, and strong enough to change how I live.
Do not let me pick and choose from your revealed will.
Teach me to value the whole gospel
its promises and its commands.
I do not want to admire grace while ignoring obedience, or obey outwardly while forgetting grace.
Make doing your will feel less like forced compliance and more like the free, glad response of a child who trusts his Father.
themes: God's revealed truth must shape both belief and practice.
The gospel includes both promises to receive and commands to obey.
Christian obedience is meant to become holy, sincere, and joyful rather than merely external.

scriptures.connection: Paul teaches that all Scripture is God-breathed and equips God's people for every good work, supporting the prayer's refusal to undervalue any part of God's revealed will.
Paul presents grace as both saving and training believers to renounce ungodliness and live upright lives, which fits the prayer's concern to hold together gospel promises and gospel obedience.
Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments, grounding the prayer's desire for obedience that is relational and sincere rather than merely formal.

movements.heading: Living faithfully in prosperity, suffering, and ordinary duties
lines: Set me apart for you in every relationship, responsibility, conversation, decision, and season of life.
If things go well for me, keep me from becoming proud or self-important.
If I suffer, keep sorrow from swallowing me whole.
Give me a balanced heart in changing circumstances.
Help me receive every duty
not as an interruption, not as a way to prove myself, but as a spiritual privilege before you.
Make me content in you, useful to others, and a life that brings honor to your name.
themes: Sanctification touches every part of life, not only private devotion.
Prosperity brings the danger of pride, and suffering brings the danger of despair.
Contentment and faithful duty can glorify God and serve as an example to others.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes learning contentment in both abundance and need through Christ's strength, directly supporting the prayer's desire for balance in prosperity and suffering.
Paul teaches that even ordinary actions are to be done for God's glory, which grounds the prayer's request to honor God in every duty and circumstance.
Paul urges Timothy to be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity, which supports the prayer's hope to become a faithful example to others.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.

movements.heading: Coming close to the great God
lines: God, you are greater than I can take in.
I come to you with reverence, but not with fear that drives me away.
You stoop down to welcome people like me, and your kindness does not lessen your glory
it shows it.
I have no claim on you.
I am unworthy, but you invite me in.
I am guilty, but you are full of mercy.
I am needy, but your riches are beyond measure.
themes: God is majestic and holy, yet merciful and near to the humble.
The believer approaches God with both reverent fear and real confidence because God welcomes sinners by grace.

scriptures.connection: This passage grounds the believer's confidence to come near to God, not in personal worthiness, but in the mercy and help given through Christ our high priest.
God is described as exalted and holy, yet also as dwelling with the contrite and lowly. That combination supports the prayer’s movement of reverence joined with confidence.

movements.heading: Resting my hope on what you have given in Christ
lines: You have shown me compassion beyond measure by giving your own Son and not holding him back.
Since you have given me Christ, I can trust you for everything I truly need in him.
He is the ground under my hope, the safe place I run to, and the open way into your presence.
Through him, show me my sin honestly, break my pride, and bring me to the end of trusting myself, so that the gospel becomes more precious to me.
themes: God’s greatest mercy is the gift of his Son for sinners.
Christ is the foundation of hope and the way into God’s presence.
True conviction of sin and self-despair make the grace of the gospel dearer, not less necessary.

scriptures.connection: Paul reasons from the Father’s gift of his Son to the believer’s confidence that God will graciously provide all that is needed in Christ.
This passage identifies Jesus’ sacrifice as the new and living way into God’s presence, matching the prayer’s confidence that access to God rests on Christ.
Paul distinguishes godly grief from despairing worldly sorrow. The prayer asks for conviction and brokenness that lead toward salvation and deeper love for the gospel.

movements.heading: Remembering the safety of belonging to Christ
lines: How blessed are those who belong to Jesus.
In him they are at peace with you, cleared of every charge that could condemn them, rescued from the wrath to come, and made heirs of a glory still ahead.
Let me live in that same hope
not lightly, but gratefully and securely, because my salvation rests in him.
themes: Union with Christ brings peace with God, justification, rescue from judgment, and inheritance of future glory.
Christian confidence is secure because it rests on Christ rather than self.

scriptures.connection: Paul links justification by faith with peace with God and access into grace, which directly supports the prayer’s confidence in Christ.
This passage speaks of believers waiting for the risen Son who delivers them from the wrath to come, echoing the prayer’s hope of rescue through Christ.
The Spirit bears witness that believers are God’s children and heirs with Christ, grounding the prayer’s language of future glory.

movements.heading: Asking for a life that shows your saving work
lines: Give me a heart that is less captivated by the world, more deeply in love with the Savior, more committed to your people, and more ready for your service.
Let these things show
not as a way to earn salvation, but as evidence that your saving grace is truly at work in me.
themes: Saving grace changes a person’s loves, loyalties, and service.
Love for Christ, detachment from the world, commitment to the church, and obedience are fruits of salvation, not the basis of it.

scriptures.connection: John warns against loving the world’s passing desires, which supports the prayer’s request for the world to lose its grip on the heart.
Grace not only saves but trains believers to renounce ungodliness and become zealous for good works. This fits the prayer’s request for visible evidence of salvation.
The call to meet together and stir one another up to love and good works supports the prayer’s desire for attachment to God’s house and people.

movements.heading: Letting my life point others to Jesus
lines: Let my character and my daily choices leave a serious, winsome impression on the people around me.
Make my life honest enough, humble enough, and kind enough that others would be drawn to ask about the way to my Master.
themes: A believer’s conduct should bear witness to Christ.
Godly character can make the gospel visible and invite others toward the Lord.

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that the visible good works of his people should lead others to glorify the Father, which supports the prayer’s desire for a life that points beyond itself.
Peter connects honorable conduct before outsiders with God being glorified, grounding the prayer’s concern that daily behavior would make a faithful impression.

movements.heading: Depending on you in everything you send
lines: Do not let anything that happens to me
whether pleasant or painful
damage the life of my soul.
Instead, use every circumstance to deepen me, steady me, and draw me nearer to you.
Send me your help.
The duties, opportunities, and means you give me are not meant to make me self-sufficient.
Even the best plans, habits, and efforts will come to nothing unless you add your blessing.
themes: God can use both joys and hardships for spiritual growth.
Believers remain dependent on God even when using the means and opportunities he provides.
Human effort and faithful means need God’s blessing to bear lasting fruit.

scriptures.connection: James teaches that trials can produce steadfastness and maturity, supporting the prayer’s request that painful events would increase rather than harm spiritual prosperity.
Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing, matching the prayer’s rejection of self-sufficiency.
Paul distinguishes human planting and watering from God giving growth, which supports the prayer’s confession that even good means are vain without God’s blessing.

movements.heading: Asking to be led by Jesus
lines: Lord Jesus, please give me the mercy of being led by you.
Teach me to pay attention to your Word and to the wise boundaries of your providence.
When you give me hard things, do not let them deaden my heart.
Use even the bitter parts of life to wake me up, sharpen my faith, and make me more alive to you.
themes: Christ personally leads his people through Scripture and providence.
Hard providences can be used by God for growth rather than spiritual collapse.
The believer asks for grace to receive suffering as under Christ's wise care.

scriptures.connection: This passage presents God's Word as the light by which his people walk, which supports the prayer's request to be directed by Scripture rather than by confusion or impulse.
James teaches that trials can produce endurance and maturity in believers, grounding the request that bitter things would enliven and strengthen faith rather than crush it.

movements.heading: Needing help when I am discouraged and tempted
lines: When I am low and unsure, give me enough encouragement to keep following you.
As you once dealt patiently with Gideon, remove what is needlessly discouraging me and give me courage for the next obedient step.
And when temptation presses in, let me hide under the shelter of your compassion, knowing you understand weakness and know how to help me.
themes: God can strengthen weak faith with patient encouragement.
Christ sympathizes with tempted believers and gives timely help.
The believer depends on Christ rather than self-confidence in temptation.

scriptures.connection: Gideon's request for signs is not presented as a model for demanding proof from God, but it does show God's patient kindness toward a fearful servant whom he is strengthening for obedience.
Hebrews grounds confidence in prayer in the sympathy of Jesus, who was tempted yet without sin, making it directly relevant to seeking help under temptation.

movements.heading: Thanking you that you have not let me go
lines: Thank you that I am still in your hand.
You have not thrown me away like a star gone dark or left me drifting like a boat with no rudder.
Keep my life in your service.
Do not let me live merely to take up space, but make my remaining days useful in the work you give me.
themes: Christ preserves his people and does not abandon them.
A believer's life is meant for God-given usefulness, not self-directed existence.
Gratitude grows from knowing one is held by Christ.

scriptures.connection: Jesus says his sheep are known, kept, and held securely in his hand, which directly supports the prayer's gratitude for not being cast off or abandoned.
Paul teaches that believers are created in Christ for good works prepared by God, grounding the desire that one's life remain useful in God's purposes.

movements.heading: Keeping me from being crushed or provoked into sin
lines: Do not let me be trampled by pride, injustice, money, status, or the selfish power of other people.
And when I am treated wrongly, keep me from anger that runs ahead of you.
Help me wait for you patiently and quietly.
Guard my mouth so I do not speak foolishly in the heat of the moment.
themes: God's people ask for protection from oppressive worldly powers and corrupt desires.
Waiting on God is an act of trust, especially under injustice.
Sinful anger and reckless speech must be resisted by grace.

scriptures.connection: This psalm calls God's people to wait for the Lord and not give way to anger over evildoers, which fits the prayer's plea for patience instead of rash outrage.
James warns that human anger does not produce God's righteousness, supporting the request for restraint in speech and temper.

movements.heading: Giving you my heart and my will
lines: Let your mercy stay with me for as long as I live.
Help me hand myself over to your will, not grudgingly, but because I trust you.
Take my heart and keep it in your hand.
Write reverence for you so deeply into me that neither time nor eternity can erase it.
themes: God's covenant mercy accompanies his people through life.
Surrender to God's will rests on trust in his goodness.
True reverence is something God writes into the heart, not something the believer can manufacture.

scriptures.connection: David's confidence that God's goodness and mercy will follow him throughout life gives biblical shape to the prayer's request for mercy to accompany the believer while living.
God promises to give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them, supporting the prayer's plea that God would take the heart and make it reverent and responsive to him.

movements.heading: Committing myself to your covenant grace
lines: I entrust myself to your grace and to the care of your covenant
in sickness and in health, in whatever comes.

I do this because you have overcome the world, fulfilled God's law, completed the righteousness that justifies sinners, swallowed up death in victory, and received all authority in heaven and on earth.
Let this covenant be marked with your own blood in the court of forgiving mercy.
Put your name on it
the name I trust
because the only signature I can bring is the weak and unworthy hand of a mortal sinner who belongs to you.
themes: The believer's confidence rests on Christ's finished saving work, not personal worthiness.
Christ's blood secures the new covenant and forgiveness of sins.
Jesus has conquered the world, defeated death, and received universal authority.
Personal commitment to God is real, but it is upheld by Christ's covenant grace.

scriptures.connection: Jesus identifies the cup with the new covenant in his blood, directly grounding the prayer's confidence that covenant mercy is sealed by Christ's blood.
Jesus tells his disciples to take heart because he has overcome the world, which supports the prayer's confidence in him amid whatever circumstances come.

Paul contrasts Adam's disobedience with Christ's obedience that brings righteousness, supporting the prayer's claim that justifying righteousness is completed in Christ rather than produced by the believer.
Paul celebrates death being swallowed up in victory through Jesus Christ, which directly supports the prayer's confidence that Christ has defeated death.
The risen Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him, grounding the prayer's trust in his universal power.

prayers.title: Coming Near to the God of Grace

movements.heading: Thanking you that I can come near
lines: Kind Lord, I praise you that you let me come to you at all.
You have opened the way for me to bring my needs, my longings, my failures, and my fears into your presence.
I do not come because I deserve a hearing, but because you are merciful and you have invited sinners like me to come to your throne of grace.
themes: God graciously welcomes sinners into his presence
Prayer is a mercy granted by God, not a right earned by human worthiness
The believer approaches God with both honesty and reverence

scriptures.connection: This passage grounds the confidence of approaching God in the priestly work of Jesus, not in personal worthiness. It specifically invites believers to come to the throne of grace for mercy and help.

movements.heading: Owning the truth about my sin
lines: I know I am not worthy of your kindness.
My heart is not what it was made to be.
Sin has bent me away from you, and it shows itself in stubbornness, disobedience, and rebellion.
Even from my earliest days, I have seen discontent, pride, envy, and the desire to get even rise up in me.
These are not small flaws;
they are signs of a heart that needs your mercy from the roots up.
themes: Human nature is corrupted by sin and needs grace at the deepest level
Personal sins reveal a deeper alienation from God
True approach to God includes honest confession rather than self-defense

scriptures.connection: Paul describes humanity apart from grace as spiritually dead and shaped by sinful desires, not merely guilty of isolated mistakes. This supports the prayer’s confession that outward sins reveal a deeper fallen condition.
This passage holds together the universality of sin and the hope of justification by grace. It fits the prayer’s movement from unworthiness toward dependence on God’s mercy.

movements.heading: Asking you not to count my past against me
lines: Please do not hold against me the sins of my youth or the many sins of the years since.
Forgive the time and gifts I have wasted.

Forgive the ways I have misused your kindness, ignored the help you placed in front of me, treated holy days and holy opportunities lightly, delayed responding to your salvation, and lived as if I did not need the Friend of sinners.
I have received more mercy than I have noticed and more light than I have followed.
themes: God is asked to pardon sins from every stage of life
Neglecting grace, worship, time, and spiritual opportunity is itself sin
Christ is the merciful friend and Savior of sinners

scriptures.connection: David asks God not to remember the sins of his youth but to remember him according to steadfast love. This directly supports the prayer’s plea for mercy over both early and later sins.
Jesus was called a friend of sinners because he received and showed mercy to those who knew their need. The prayer’s phrase points to Christ’s gracious welcome, not approval of sin.

movements.heading: Letting conviction lead me to Christ, not despair
lines: As I confess my guilt, please do not let me treat it lightly.
Help me feel the seriousness of my sin before you.
Bring me to the end of trusting myself, my excuses, or my own goodness.
But do not let that end in hopelessness.
Teach me to look to you, where there is real hope, and to see Jesus, the Lamb of God, who takes away sin.
themes: True conviction includes grief over sin without abandoning hope in God
Self-despair means giving up confidence in self-righteousness, not denying God’s mercy
Jesus is the Lamb whose sacrifice deals with sin

scriptures.connection: Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief that leads to death. This supports the prayer’s request for deep conviction that moves toward God rather than away from him.
John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away sin. This is the central hope the prayer asks to see in the middle of confession.

movements.heading: Bringing me back through Jesus
lines: Through Jesus, bring me back to yourself.
Make me willing to listen when you speak, to trust you when I cannot see the whole road, to love what you command, and to obey you from the heart.
Hold me up when I am weak, because I cannot keep myself close to you by my own strength.
themes: Return to God is through Christ
Faith, obedience, delight in God’s law, and perseverance are gifts to be sought from God
The believer depends on God to be upheld

scriptures.connection: Jesus teaches that access to the Father comes through him. This grounds the prayer’s request to return to God through Christ rather than through self-effort.
The psalmist asks God to teach, incline, and turn his heart toward God’s ways. This supports the prayer’s desire not only to know God’s commands but to delight in and obey them.

movements.heading: Keeping my whole life clean and useful
lines: Guard my mind from falsehood, my loves from idols, my mouth from deceit, and my actions from what is corrupt.
Keep my reputation from anything that would dishonor you or confuse others.
Make my life harmless, honest, and above reproach.
Let me become steady, useful, wise, and generous with the light you give me.
Give me real zeal for your glory and real love for the good of the people around me.
themes: God’s grace trains the whole person: mind, desires, speech, conduct, and public witness
Holiness is meant to be visible, humble, and useful to others
Zeal for God’s glory should be joined to love for neighbor

scriptures.connection: Paul calls believers to live blamelessly and shine as lights in a crooked generation while holding fast to the word of life. This directly supports the prayer’s desire for a life that is above reproach and light-giving.
Peter connects honorable conduct before others with God being glorified. This supports the prayer’s concern that character and public witness serve God’s glory and the good of others.
Paul applies new life in Christ to truthful speech, rejecting corruption, and using words to build others up. This grounds the prayer’s requests about lips, conduct, and usefulness.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Seeing life from the edge of eternity
lines: Lord, when I pray, you draw me out beyond the smallness of this present life.
I begin to see the world differently.
The things that usually impress me, distract me, or crush me lose their weight.
The pleasures that promise so much and the disappointments that hurt so deeply are not ultimate.
In your presence, I remember that I am small, that you are eternal, and that my life only makes sense when it is lived for you.
themes: Prayer brings the believer into conscious fellowship with the eternal God.
Eternal perspective relativizes earthly pleasures, disappointments, and fears.
Humility grows when the soul sees God as he is.

scriptures.connection: Paul contrasts visible, temporary afflictions with unseen eternal glory. This supports the prayer’s movement from the pressures of mortal life into a God-given eternal perspective.
Believers are called to set their minds on things above because their life is hidden with Christ. This grounds the prayer’s desire to see ordinary life in light of eternity.

movements.heading: Being carried by the Spirit toward home
lines: Thank you for the Holy Spirit, who carries me when I do not have strength in myself.
Let him fill my praying with fresh longing for you.
Keep moving me toward the city you have promised, where your people will live with you forever.
Make my heart thirsty to belong to you more fully, not just in words, but with my whole life.
themes: The Holy Spirit helps and strengthens believers in prayer.
The Christian life is pilgrimage toward the heavenly city.
True prayer awakens longing for deeper holiness and fuller communion with God.

scriptures.connection: Paul teaches that the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes according to God’s will. This directly supports the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit in prayer.
Hebrews describes believers as having come to the heavenly Jerusalem through Christ. This illuminates the prayer’s hope of being carried toward the promised city of God.

movements.heading: Letting lesser things fall away
lines: When I am with you in prayer, the things below stop looking so large.
What matters most becomes clearer:
a heart made holy before you, and people brought safely to Christ.
My worries, fears, and anxious thoughts shrink in your hands.
They are real, but they are not lord over me.
You are.
themes: Prayer reorders loves and priorities around holiness and salvation.
God’s presence gives peace that displaces anxiety.
Earthly cares are brought under God’s rule rather than denied.

scriptures.connection: Paul tells believers to bring anxieties to God in prayer, with the promise of God’s peace guarding them. This supports the section’s movement from fear and care into trustful prayer.
Jesus teaches his disciples not to be ruled by anxious concern, but to seek God’s kingdom and righteousness first. This fits the prayer’s shift from worldly concerns to holiness and salvation.

movements.heading: Rejoicing in what you are doing in your church
lines: Father, give me joy in what you are doing among your people.
Make me glad when your church is built up, when sinners come home to you, and when your name becomes great because of mercy shown to people who did not deserve it.
Let me care more about your kingdom than my reputation, comfort, or success.
themes: God glorifies his name by saving sinners and gathering them to himself.
The believer’s joy is enlarged by God’s work in the church.
Prayer aligns personal desires with the coming of God’s kingdom.

scriptures.connection: Jesus says heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. This grounds the prayer’s joy and longing over sinners returning to God.
Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for God’s name to be honored and his kingdom to come. This supports the section’s desire that God’s name be made great through his saving work.

movements.heading: Putting myself and my concerns in your hands
lines: In prayer, lift me above both criticism and praise.
Let neither people’s rejection nor their approval control me.
Give me a taste of the joy that belongs to your kingdom, so that I can hand myself over to you without holding anything back.
I place my concerns, plans, desires, and future in your hands.
Do with me what is right and good.
I do not want to live as if my will were the center of everything.
I want to be yours, completely and forever.
themes: Prayer frees believers from bondage to human approval.
Surrender means entrusting the whole self and future to God’s wise will.
Heavenly joy strengthens wholehearted devotion to God.

scriptures.connection: Paul contrasts seeking human approval with being a servant of Christ. This supports the prayer’s desire to be lifted above both flattery and disapproval.
Paul calls believers to offer themselves to God as living sacrifices and be transformed in mind. This grounds the prayer’s language of placing the whole self at God’s disposal.

movements.heading: Praying freely for others as your child
lines: Father, teach me to pray freely for others:
for my friends, for those who lead and serve your church, for people who do not yet know you, for your whole church, and for your kingdom to come in this world.
Let me come to you honestly and warmly, as your child speaking to a good Father, with deep affection for you and real hope in what you can do.
themes: Believers are invited to intercede broadly for others.
Christian prayer is both reverent and intimate because God is Father.
Hopeful intercession rests on God’s saving desire and kingdom purposes.

scriptures.connection: Paul urges prayers and intercessions for all kinds of people and connects this with God’s saving purposes. This supports praying for friends, leaders, sinners, and the wider world.
Believers receive the Spirit of adoption and cry to God as Father. This grounds the section’s confidence and openness before God as his child.

movements.heading: Making my life prayerful
lines: Lord, do not let prayer be only something I visit and then leave behind.
Make me a person who keeps turning toward you.
Teach me to pray in the middle of ordinary life, to depend on you without stopping, and to live each day in steady conversation with you.
themes: Prayer is not only an activity but a continuing posture of dependence on God.
Believers are called to persistent prayer in all circumstances.
A life of prayer expresses ongoing communion with God.

scriptures.connection: Paul commands believers to pray without ceasing and give thanks in all circumstances. This directly supports the prayer’s final request to become continually prayerful.
Paul calls believers to pray at all times in the Spirit with perseverance for all the saints. This supports both continual prayer and intercession for the church.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Learning to bring everything to you
lines: God, you hear me when I come to you.
Teach me to live not only by accepting what you provide and allow, but by actually bringing my life to you in prayer
my soul, my body, my children, my family, and my church.
Make my heart willing to be shaped by what you want.
Let prayer become the way I live before you, so that I honor you and am guarded from evil, including the evil I do not even recognize in myself.
themes: God welcomes prayer; prayer belongs in every part of ordinary life; God’s providence and prayer are not enemies but belong together; the heart needs to be shaped by God’s will; God protects his people from seen and unseen evil.

scriptures.connection: Paul tells believers to bring every concern to God with prayer and thanksgiving, and he connects that prayer with God’s guarding peace. This supports the prayer’s desire to bring all of life before God rather than live self-sufficiently.

Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for God’s name, kingdom, will, daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil. That pattern grounds the prayer’s movement from daily dependence to surrender and protection.

movements.heading: Seeing my sin without losing sight of your good purposes
lines: Help me see honestly that sin clings even to the good things I do.
Keep me from pretending my motives are cleaner than they are.
At the same time, teach me to receive something good from everything you put in my path.
Even when circumstances expose what is wrong in me, use them to draw me nearer to you and make me wiser in your ways.
themes: The believer remains dependent on grace because sin still affects motives and actions; God can use all circumstances, including humbling ones, for spiritual good; self-knowledge should lead to dependence rather than despair.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes the painful reality that sin remains present even when he desires to do good, and he turns from self-reliance to deliverance through Christ. This supports the prayer’s honest confession that sin accompanies even good actions.
Paul teaches that God works all things for the good of those who love him, with that good defined by conformity to Christ. This grounds the request to gain spiritual good from whatever God allows.

movements.heading: Letting prayer change my will, not trying to manage yours
lines: Teach me that prayer is not my way of bending you to my plans.
Its work is to bring my will into line with yours.
When I pray as if you must agree with me, I am acting as though I know better than Christ.
That is pride, and I confess it as sin.
Save me from using prayer to stay in control while pretending to trust you.
themes: Prayer is an act of submission, not control; Christ is Lord and wiser than the believer; pride can corrupt even religious activity; true prayer seeks God’s will above personal preference.

scriptures.connection: In Gethsemane, Jesus brings his real desire to the Father while submitting himself to the Father’s will. His prayer gives the pattern for honest petition joined to surrender.
James warns that prayer can be disordered by selfish desires. This directly supports the confession that prayer becomes sinful when it is used to serve my own agenda rather than God’s will.

movements.heading: Praying by what you command and promise
lines: Keep me praying according to what you have told me to ask for and what you have promised to give.
I do not need to force your hand.
I need to trust your word and leave myself in your hands.
When you command me to ask for forgiveness, peace, and a broken and teachable heart, you are not mocking me.
You call me to ask because you are willing to give what brings glory to you and real good to me.
themes: Prayer rests on God’s commands and promises; God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; forgiveness, peace, and repentance are gifts God delights to give; God’s glory and the believer’s good belong together.

scriptures.connection: John teaches confidence in prayer when believers ask according to God’s will. This grounds the prayer’s emphasis on praying by God’s revealed will rather than by presumption.
John connects confession with God’s faithful forgiveness and cleansing. This supports the confidence that when God calls me to seek pardon, he is ready to give it in Christ.
God promises to give his people a new heart and Spirit-led obedience. This illuminates the request for brokenness and a heart made responsive to God.

movements.heading: Asking boldly for more than small comforts
lines: Do not let my prayers shrink down to only small personal comforts.
Give me holy boldness to ask for great things
for your people and for me
not so that we can look impressive, but so that our lives would make your glory visible.
Make me willing to want what would honor you most, even when it stretches my faith and exposes how small my desires have become.
themes: Believers are invited to pray boldly; prayer should seek the good of God’s people as well as personal needs; the ultimate aim of answered prayer is God’s glory; faith expands desire beyond private comfort.

scriptures.connection: Paul praises God as able to do far more than believers ask or imagine, and he connects that abundance to God’s glory in the church and in Christ. This supports asking boldly for great things for God’s people.
Jesus links abiding in him with effective prayer, fruitfulness, and the Father’s glory. This grounds the desire that answered prayer would produce lives that display God’s glory.

movements.heading: Coming freely, remembering your ways, and refusing my own cravings
lines: Teach me that it is wise to pray about everything I have and everything I need
not because I am forced to, but because I love you and belong to you.
Let me come to you at any time and lay my needs open before you without fear.
My great sin is how easily I lose the taste and weight of your ways.
Bring that truth back to my mind, because remembering it helps me live aware of your nearness.
And Father, do not hand me over to myself.
There is no misery like being ruled by my own desires for my own ends.
Govern me by your Spirit instead, and teach me to want what leads to life.
themes: Prayer is free access to the Father through grace; love, not mere necessity, should draw the believer to God; forgetting the beauty of God’s ways dulls awareness of his presence; being ruled by sinful desires is a severe form of judgment; the Spirit’s rule leads to life.

scriptures.connection: Because of Christ our high priest, believers are invited to approach God’s throne with confidence for mercy and help. This supports coming freely and honestly with needs at any time.

Jesus connects love for him, keeping his commandments, and the experience of his self-disclosure to the believer. This supports the idea that treasuring and remembering God’s ways is tied to a living sense of his presence.

Paul describes God’s judgment as giving people over to the desires they have chosen in exchange for God. This grounds the prayer’s severe warning that being ruled by one’s own lusts is itself a terrible form of wrath.

Paul contrasts living by the flesh with putting sin to death by the Spirit, and identifies those led by the Spirit as God’s children. This supports the final request to be governed by the Spirit rather than by sinful desires.

movements.heading: Let my whole life become prayer
lines: Great God, whether I am with your people or alone, at church or at home, let my life be soaked in prayer.
Teach me to come to you again and again, not trusting my own words, but trusting the blood of Jesus that makes sinners welcome.
Help me and protect me as long as I am still living here by faith, until the day prayer gives way to unhindered praise in your presence.
themes: A life of continual prayer depends on grace, not performance.
Access to God is made possible through Christ's atoning blood.
Earthly prayer anticipates the unbroken worship of eternity.

scriptures.connection: This passage grounds the believer's confidence to draw near to God in the blood of Jesus and his priestly work, which directly supports the prayer's dependence on atonement rather than personal worthiness.
The promise of a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy gives biblical language for prayer being stirred up by God's own gracious work, not merely by human effort.
The vision of God's servants worshiping him in the new creation illuminates the prayer's hope that present praying will one day become unbroken praise.

movements.heading: I come because I need you and because you invite me
lines: I come to you because I am needy, because your promises call me, and because your Spirit draws me.
I do not want to treat your presence casually.
You are holy, majestic, great, and glorious.
Still, I do not run away from you, because your love gives me courage to come close.
themes: God is approached with reverent fear because he is holy and glorious.
God's promises and the Spirit's work encourage believers to come near.
The Father's love gives confidence without removing reverence.

scriptures.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers are invited to approach God's throne for mercy and help; this holds together deep need and real confidence.
Paul teaches that the Spirit enables believers to approach God as Father, which supports the prayer's movement from fear of God's greatness to courage in his love.
This text speaks of God as greatly feared and held in awe among his people, grounding the prayer's reverence before God's majesty.

movements.heading: I have nothing to pay, so I hold on to Jesus
lines: Before you, I am poor and guilty.
I have nothing of my own that could repay you or balance what I owe.
But by faith I hold on to Jesus.
I place his righteousness where my sins stand against me.
I have nothing to put on my side of the scale, but he is more than enough.
His obedience, his blood, and his finished work satisfy your justice for me.
themes: Human beings have no spiritual wealth with which to pay their debt before God.
Faith rests on Christ's righteousness rather than personal merit.
Christ's atonement satisfies divine justice for sinners.

scriptures.connection: Paul rejects any righteousness of his own and wants to be found in Christ with the righteousness that comes through faith, which closely matches the prayer's plea to be represented by Christ's righteousness.
This passage explains that God justifies sinners through Christ's redemption and propitiation while remaining just, directly supporting the claim that Christ satisfies God's justice.
Paul describes the exchange in which Christ bears sin so that believers become righteous in him, illuminating the prayer's confidence that Jesus stands in the place of the guilty.

movements.heading: My sin is serious, but your mercy in Christ is deeper
lines: I praise you that my great sin has not exhausted your grace.
I know even the sins I call small deserve your judgment, because they are sins against you, the infinite and holy God.
But there is mercy for me in Christ.
Where my guilt is most frightening, your mercy in him is free, deep, and stronger than my sin.
themes: Sin is measured by the holiness of the God it offends.
Grace does not minimize guilt; it overcomes guilt in Christ.
God's mercy is especially displayed in forgiving serious sinners through Jesus.

scriptures.connection: Paul teaches that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, which directly supports the prayer's praise that great guilt draws out the greatness of grace in Christ.
David confesses that sin is ultimately against God, grounding the prayer's insistence that even sin people consider small is deeply serious because of who God is.
Paul presents himself as a great sinner who received mercy as a display of Christ's patience, supporting the prayer's confidence that terrible guilt does not put a sinner beyond mercy.

movements.heading: Show me more of Christ and speak peace to my heart
lines: Bless me by showing me more of the saving worth of Jesus.
Let me see your goodness more clearly.
Speak peace to my broken and repentant heart, not because I have made myself clean, but because Christ is enough for me.
themes: Believers need God to reveal more of Christ's saving sufficiency.
God's goodness is known as he makes himself known to his people.
Peace with God comes through Christ, especially to the contrite who cast themselves on mercy.

scriptures.connection: Moses asks to see God's glory, and God responds by proclaiming his goodness; this supports the prayer's request for God to make his goodness known.
Paul states that justification by faith brings peace with God through Jesus Christ, grounding the prayer's request for peace in Christ's sufficiency rather than self-improvement.
The psalm teaches that God does not despise a broken and contrite heart, which fits the prayer's plea for peace spoken to a repentant heart.

movements.heading: Do not let me stop seeking you until Christ rules all of me
lines: Keep me praying and refusing to let go until Christ rules every part of me
every thought, every word, every action.
Give me the kind of faith that cleanses my heart, overcomes the pull of the world, shows itself in love, fastens me to you, and keeps me clinging to the cross.
themes: The goal of prayer is not only pardon but Christ's practical rule in the whole life.
Saving faith purifies, perseveres, overcomes the world, and works through love.
Growth in holiness depends on continuing dependence on Christ and his cross.

scriptures.connection: Paul calls believers not to let sin reign but to present themselves to God under grace, supporting the prayer's longing for Christ to rule thought, speech, and conduct.
This verse describes faith working through love, which directly supports the prayer's desire for a living faith that expresses itself in love.
John says faith is the victory that overcomes the world, grounding the prayer's request for faith that resists the world's power.
The call to run with endurance while looking to Jesus supports the prayer's desire to keep clinging to Christ and persevering in holiness.

movements.heading: Coming to the God whose name is love
lines: Gracious Lord, you are love, so please receive this prayer in love.
My sins feel too many to count
more than the sand along the sea.
But your grace is greater than my sin.
Where I have multiplied guilt, you have poured out mercy beyond measure.
Please do not deal with me according to what I deserve.
Receive me because of who you are, and because your mercy does not run dry.
themes: God is love; human sin is real and abundant; grace is more abundant than sin; the sinner approaches God only by mercy.

scriptures.connection: John grounds God's love not in human worthiness but in God's sending of his Son as the atoning sacrifice. That directly supports approaching God as love while honestly confessing sin.
Paul teaches that grace does not merely match sin but overflows beyond it through Jesus Christ. This anchors the prayer's confidence that even countless sins are not greater than God's grace.

movements.heading: Resting my forgiveness on Christ
lines: Father, look on the cross of your beloved Son.
See the worth of his blood given for sinners like me.
Hear him as he speaks for me even now.
Let the truth of the gospel reach my own heart:
my sins are forgiven in Christ.
Teach me to take courage, to stop pretending I can pay my own debt, and to lie down in peace because Jesus has carried what I could never carry.
themes: Forgiveness rests on Christ's atoning death and ongoing intercession; assurance and peace come from the finished work of Christ, not self-payment.

scriptures.connection: Hebrews presents Jesus as the living priest who saves completely because he continually intercedes for those who draw near to God through him. This supports the prayer's appeal to Christ's never-failing intercession.
John holds together honest sinfulness with Christ's advocacy and atoning sacrifice. That is the foundation for asking God to speak forgiveness and peace to the conscience.

movements.heading: Learning to treasure prayer
lines: Your grace pours down like a waterfall from heaven, and your mercy never gets tired of doing good.
Help me value the gift of prayer more and more.
Teach me to come to you as I really am:
stained by sin, needing pardon, and yet invited to speak with you.
Let prayer become part of my whole life with you

the path under my feet, the hand on the door before my lips open, the light by which I see, the sound that tunes my ears, the life inside my understanding, the strength of my choices, the fire of my love, and the sweetness of what I remember.
themes: Prayer is a privilege of access to God for sinners who need pardon; communion with God should shape the whole person—speech, perception, understanding, will, affections, and memory.

scriptures.connection: Because Jesus is the great high priest, believers may draw near to God's throne for mercy and grace. This supports the prayer's confidence that a sinful person may come honestly to God and find help.
David's prayer shows desire for God affecting the whole person—soul, body, lips, memory, and trust. It illuminates the request that prayer would shape every faculty of life.

movements.heading: Asking to pray in a way that pleases you
lines: Shape the things I ask for.
Keep my prayers wise, humble, surrendered, obedient to you, formed by Scripture, and made more like Jesus.
Save me from praying as if I were trying to manage you.
Teach me to ask honestly, but also to trust your will more than my own.
themes: Prayer should be governed by humility, obedience, Scripture, submission to God's will, and conformity to Christ rather than selfish control.

scriptures.connection: John connects confidence in prayer with asking according to God's will. This supports the desire for prayers that are submissive and shaped by God's purposes.
Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane models honest petition joined to complete surrender to the Father's will. This grounds the request to pray in a Christ-like way.
James warns that prayer can be distorted by selfish motives. That helps explain the request for wise and humble desires in prayer.

movements.heading: Trusting that you answer better than I can ask
lines: Give me steady faith that prayer is never wasted.
When I do not receive what I asked for, keep me from thinking you have ignored me.
Teach me to believe that your answer may be larger, richer, and wiser than what I could see at the time.
Before I ever knew to ask, you gave me your greatest gift:
your Son.
Since you have given me Christ, help me trust that, in him, you will give me everything I truly need.
themes: God hears prayer; apparent denial may be wise providence; the gift of Christ guarantees God's fatherly provision for all that is truly needed.

scriptures.connection: Paul praises God as able to do beyond what believers ask or imagine. This supports trusting that God's answers may exceed the form of the original request.
Paul argues from the greater gift to the lesser: the Father who did not spare his Son will graciously give what his people need. This directly grounds the prayer's closing confidence.

movements.heading: Coming to you where mercy is given
lines: Father, it is a gift that I can come near to you at all.
Because of Jesus, your throne is not a place I need to run from, but the place where my soul finds mercy, welcome, and help.
Here I remember that you are not against me in Christ.
Here I can ask boldly, not because I deserve anything, but because Jesus has opened the way.
themes: Access to God is possible through Christ; the believer approaches God’s throne as a place of grace, mercy, reconciliation, and help rather than terror.

scriptures.connection: This passage grounds the prayer’s confidence in coming to God’s throne for mercy and timely help, because Jesus is the great high priest who represents his people before the Father.
Paul connects peace with God and access into grace directly to justification through Jesus Christ, supporting the prayer’s sense of God’s reconciled welcome.

movements.heading: Receiving what I need for the fight
lines: When I come to you, you strengthen me for what I face.
Teach me to take up your Word as my weapon, to trust you as my shield, and to live in the safety of the salvation you have given me.
Feed me from Scripture when I am empty.
Give me endurance for the road ahead, courage for temptation, and strength to stand when enemies within and around me press hard.
themes: God equips his people through his Word, faith, salvation, and spiritual strength for endurance, temptation, and conflict.

scriptures.connection: Paul describes the believer’s conflict and God’s provision of spiritual armor, including faith, salvation, and the Word of God, which closely matches this section’s petitions.
The Christian life is pictured as a race requiring endurance, with eyes fixed on Jesus; this supports the prayer’s request for strength to keep going upward and forward.

movements.heading: Turning to Christ as the source of every blessing
lines: Lord Jesus, every good gift I need comes through you.
You are not a small stream of mercy but an overflowing source.
And still I confess how foolish I am:
with grace so near, I often leave it untouched.
I stay dull, prayerless, distracted, and slow to reach for what you freely give.
For the honour of your name, have mercy on this lifelessness in me.
themes: Christ is the abundant source of grace and blessing; the believer confesses spiritual dullness and failure to receive what God freely offers.

scriptures.connection: John speaks of believers receiving grace from Christ’s fullness, which supports the prayer’s picture of Christ as the overflowing source of divine blessing.
Paul locates every spiritual blessing in Christ, grounding the prayer’s claim that the gifts needed for life with God come through him.
The psalmist confesses a soul brought low and asks God for life according to his Word, fitting the prayer’s plea for mercy in spiritual deadness.

movements.heading: Asking you to wake me up and keep me close
lines: Holy Spirit, wake me up.
Stir my heart.
Fill me with a clean and steady zeal for God.
Make me hold on to you and not drift away.
Draw from the Father’s hand everything I need, and teach me to receive it with faith.
I know myself:
if I am not growing, I am sliding backward.
Keep me close, dependent, and alive to you.
themes: The Holy Spirit enlivens, strengthens, and keeps the believer dependent on God; spiritual life requires ongoing growth rather than complacency.

scriptures.connection: Paul presents life by the Spirit as the alternative to being ruled by the flesh, and he calls believers to keep in step with the Spirit, which supports the prayer’s longing for Spirit-led vitality.
This passage holds together the believer’s active obedience and God’s inward work, fitting the prayer’s request for strength to cling to God while depending on him to work within.

Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him and that apart from him believers can do nothing, supporting the concern that spiritual life cannot remain healthy without ongoing communion with Christ.

movements.heading: Living humbly with eternity in view
lines: Keep me humble about the good I have failed to do and the wrong I have actually done.
Press into my mind that my time here is short, that there is work you have given me, that I will answer to you, and that eternity is near.
Make me afraid of treating your Spirit lightly.
Do not let me forget that nothing in me is hidden from you:
you see, you hear, and you know the whole truth.
themes: Awareness of sin, mortality, accountability before God, and the danger of resisting the Spirit should produce humility and sober obedience.

scriptures.connection: Paul urges careful living because the days are evil and calls believers to understand the Lord’s will, which supports the prayer’s concern for short time and faithful work.
This passage teaches that all must appear before Christ’s judgment seat, grounding the prayer’s sober awareness that an account will be rendered to God.
The writer emphasizes that all creatures are exposed before God, which supports the prayer’s reminder that God sees and knows everything.
Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, which gives biblical weight to the prayer’s fear of treating the Spirit’s work with contempt or indifference.

movements.heading: Not letting go until Christ fills my life
lines: Father, do not let me settle for distant religion or occasional thoughts of you.
Teach me to keep asking, seeking, and knocking until Christ is at the center of me:
the life-beat of my heart, the truth that shapes my words, and the light that guides my next step.
Make him not only the one I believe in, but the one who governs how I love, speak, choose, and walk today.
themes: The believer longs for Christ to rule the heart, speech, and daily obedience, and persists in prayer for deeper conformity to him.

scriptures.connection: Jesus encourages persistent asking, seeking, and knocking because the Father gives good gifts to his children, supporting the prayer’s holy refusal to stop seeking deeper life in Christ.
Paul calls believers to let Christ’s word dwell richly in them and to do everything in his name, which supports the prayer’s desire for Christ to shape speech and daily action.
The psalm describes God’s Word as light for the path, fitting the prayer’s request that Christ guide the believer’s steps through his truth.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
provenance.copyrightStatus: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
provenance.adaptationNote: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

movements.heading: Keep my life from making the gospel look ugly
lines: O God, please do not let my life become empty, useless, or harmful.
Keep me from living in a way that gives people a reason to mock your truth.
When I enjoy the freedom you have given me in Christ, do not let me twist it into an excuse for selfishness or sin.
Teach me to use my freedom to love and serve people, not to indulge myself.
themes: Christian freedom is not permission to sin but a call to loving service.
A believer’s conduct can either commend or dishonor the truth of the gospel.
The Christian life should be fruitful rather than spiritually empty.

scriptures.connection: Paul directly connects Christian freedom with serving one another through love, warning believers not to use liberty as an opportunity for the flesh. This grounds the prayer’s concern that freedom in Christ be used for holiness and love rather than self-indulgence.

Paul urges believers, especially those who teach or represent the faith, to live with integrity so that opponents have no legitimate reason to speak evil. This supports the request that the pray-er’s life not bring reproach on the way of truth.

movements.heading: Make my faith beautiful in ordinary relationships
lines: Father, help me care not only about being technically right, but also about being gracious, wise, and good to be around.
Teach me to seek what builds my neighbor up.
Let my faith show itself in patience, kindness, humility, and steady love.
Make my life with you both true and winsome, so that what I say about the gospel is backed up by the kind of person I am becoming.
themes: Love for neighbor is a central expression of obedience to God.
Christian maturity includes both essential truth and the beauty of Christlike character.
The gospel should be made visible through conduct as well as words.

scriptures.connection: Paul calls believers not to live merely to please themselves, but to seek their neighbor’s good and upbuilding. That is the heart of this section’s request for a faith that serves and strengthens others.

Paul directs the church to give attention to what is honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, and worthy of praise, and to practice what they have learned. This supports the prayer’s concern for what is not only doctrinally essential but also beautiful and commendable in Christian life.
Paul says faithful conduct can adorn the doctrine of God our Savior. This gives biblical shape to the request that the pray-er’s profession of faith be attractive rather than harsh or off-putting.

movements.heading: Let my whole life point people toward Jesus
lines: Lord Jesus, help me speak of your way not only with my words but with my tone, my reactions, my habits, and my choices.
Let my life and my lips tell the same story.

When I meet people along the road, give me courage and warmth to say, in whatever way is fitting, that I am heading toward the place you have promised, and that there is good for them in coming with me to you.
themes: Witness includes both verbal testimony and embodied holiness.
Christians are pilgrims moving toward God’s promised future.
Evangelism is an invitation to share in the good God gives through Christ.

scriptures.connection: Peter joins readiness to speak about hope with gentleness, respect, and a good conscience. This fits the prayer’s desire to bear witness to Jesus with both speech and manner of life.
Jesus teaches that visible good works should lead others to glorify the Father. This supports the request that the pray-er’s conduct, not only words, point people toward God.
Moses invites Hobab to come with Israel because the Lord has promised good to his people. The prayer echoes that pilgrim invitation: come with me toward the good God has promised.

movements.heading: Prepare me for this short and uncertain life
lines: Father, this life is brief, changeable, and not under my control.
Prepare me for whatever you appoint for me.
While I am here, make me useful.
As I travel through this life, give me the comfort that comes from trusting you.
And when the time comes for me to leave this world, carry me safely through death into the life you have promised.
themes: Human life is brief and uncertain, so wisdom and readiness are needed.
God’s providence governs the believer’s circumstances.
The believer can face death with hope because life with Christ continues beyond the grave.

scriptures.connection: James reminds believers that they do not control tomorrow and should live under the Lord’s will. This grounds the prayer’s sober acceptance of life’s uncertainty and dependence on God’s appointments.
Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days so they may gain wisdom. That supports the prayer’s desire to live usefully and wisely within a short life.
Paul views both living and dying in relation to Christ, with death bringing him to be with Christ. This illuminates the request for a safe passage out of this life and hope beyond death.

movements.heading: Make me useful, steady, and unashamed
lines: Make me, by your grace, refreshing where people are weary, preserving where things are decaying, and clear where there is darkness.
Let the life of Christ in me overflow for the good of others.
Keep me from being ashamed of Jesus or of his words.
Do not let fear stop me from doing what I know is right, and do not let my weakness make me give up before I obey.
Teach me to trust your strength more than my own.
themes: Believers are called to be salt and light in the world.
Christian usefulness comes from God’s life and grace, not self-sufficiency.
Faithfulness requires courage when obedience is costly or weakness is felt.

scriptures.connection: Jesus names his disciples the salt of the earth and the light of the world, tying their visible lives to the Father’s glory. This directly supports the prayer’s desire to have a preserving and illuminating presence in the world.
Jesus speaks of living water flowing from those who come to him, referring to the Spirit. This supports the request that the life God gives would overflow from the believer for the good of others.

Paul tells Timothy that God gives not fear but power, love, and self-control, and urges him not to be ashamed of testimony about the Lord. This closely fits the prayer’s plea for courage in known duty despite fear or weakness.

movements.heading: Use everything to make me ready for what is next
lines: God, teach me to see my life in your light.
Shape my judgment so I can understand things truly, and shape my heart so that what I understand makes me more holy.

Use your fatherly discipline, your providence, your Word, prayer, worship, and the life of your people to prepare me for the duties still ahead of me, for the serious hour when I must die, and for the joy and service that wait beyond the grave.
themes: God gives wisdom and moral clarity by his light and Word.
Providential discipline is part of God’s fatherly work of holiness.
God uses ordinary means of grace to prepare believers for faithful life, death, and eternal service.

scriptures.connection: The psalm confesses that true light is found in God’s light. This supports the request to see all things rightly because God himself gives the light by which reality is understood.

Hebrews describes God’s discipline as painful but purposeful, producing holiness and righteousness. This grounds the prayer’s desire that providential hardships would sanctify rather than embitter the believer.
Paul teaches that Scripture equips the person of God for every good work. This supports the request that God’s appointed means would prepare the pray-er for remaining duties.
John’s vision of the new creation includes God’s servants serving him in his presence. This gives biblical support to the prayer’s hope for joy and service beyond the grave.

provenance.originalAuthor: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
provenance.originalSource: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
